INTRUDING BASE BOARDS AND BELLOWS. In many cases when using field cameras, especially when working with their wide-angle lenses, and when using the rising front or the side swing, amateurs find that a portion of the plate shows on development a border, more or less broad, of a rather transparent film. This often is a 'puzzle to the beginner, but it simply means that either the base board of the damera or a rart of the bellows has come in the way of the light. If the base-board cuts off the picture in this way, the only remedy is to miave the camera back and front further forward, or to have the camera altered. If the citt-off is caused by the bellows, it will often be found that they are sagging towards the plate, and that by drawing them forwatd towards the front board, the cut-off will be cured. The main moral of this paragraph is that Fben photographing wide- angle subjects, or when lasing extreme rise or fall of front, it is always necessary to see that the image extends properly to the edge of the plate.

something quickly. inside." "I feel you are most kind," he rued. "I confess it was a trespass even to get a photograph of your beautiful old house. I shall be thankful for doctoring, though I feel I don't deserve it." , He followed the pair through the gate and , on to the principal door. If he was enamoured of the house from without, what he now saw completely captivated him. The room he en- tered was 'panelled in oak to the ceiling, and made a perfect setting for the inmates, whom the visitor summed up already as being no ordinary country folk. In addition to the mother and daughter was another occupant, pathetic alike in pose and expression. It was a very aged man, seated in .an arm chair near the fireless hearth. AR Lifson entered, he turned ' hit head suddenly, and looked keenly at him, exhibiting a beauti- fully fine acquiline face. A movement, as though about to rise, was checked by the younger lady, who went to him and spoke some- thing softly, which caused him to relapse into his old attitude. In obedience to the mistress's direction, Litson seated himself near the window, where the in- ' flamed cheek received attention. During the operation his other eye was quizzing the girl standing near, assisting her mother,- and now and then exchanging a quick glance with the owner of the disengaged eye. Both made estimates. His of her—a rather short figure, but by nature. elegant. A face almost boyish, an arch mirth- fulness its chief characteristic. 'Hair curly, in- capable of much restraint, matching in colour her clear, brown eyes, that seemed always inquir- ing. by reason of her arched eyebrows. Although plainly dressed, her frock worn to a degree of shabbiness, a style about her from head to foot, rendering her decidedly distinguished, height- ened by the natty white kerchief which fitted the charming line of her shoulders and bust, reveal- ing the darkish blue bodice underneath. As she stood, her head set at ,a quizzical angle, her hands behind her back, her lips slightly apart, this young gentleman, a leading member of a noted London theatrical company, sent into the country by the doctors for change and rest, thought of half-a-dozen plays' in which, so far as Looks wont, she would fit a character to a T. From her standpoint she thought she had never seen another face like his. Thin to a de.. groe, and pale, and at times almost expression- less; but when its owner looked at you or re- sponded to your glance,it was like a quick-change artiste, and you marvelled at its mobility. The doctoring, as he described the treatment 'of his eye, was a somewhat elaborate process, and when he at last arose from his seat with a layer of housewife's blue anointing his cheek. bono, with instructions not to wipe it off just yet, the situation was too much for the young lady. For Lifson made such a comic picture as to move her to laughter. But he liked the musics of these bells so much that he tried to produce more, and succeeded by reciting in the most irre- sistible manner an impromptu to this Offect, the doleful pitch of his voice equalling the gravity of his oountenance: "How doth the much too busy bee, Improve our eyes and noses, By poking in his antennas. Mistaking us for posies." The young lady, after her laughter, addressed a word to him for the first time. "And pray, sir; for what flower might the bees have mistaken' you ? " "Plainly, for fcrget-mO-nots. I carry the blue in my eye and the sentiment in my heart."

The weather in the month following was quite justifying November's ill-repute. Godiva had made it her business of late to take a look round the steading 'after nightfall. She and her mother had noticed the strange circumstance of William's early absence at times the last week or so It was one Saturday night, when, in accord- ance with her recent custom, she was visiting every place where there was live-stork. The hour was full of moan and woe. The beautiful autumn tints had given place to dank •decay ; the 1 air was charged with mist and drizzle. Ragged clouds were beating rapidly across the sky, where a waning half-moon .was playing hide- and-seek with the world below. Flickering opal lights were reflected intermittently in the waste of waters--the mores made by the over-brim- min°. Bicker. The water had spread over the orchard, which sloped down to it, but had parted with its low fence, years ago, and now, this autumn, had parted with a large quantity of earth also, the undermining process having- gone on fdr years. 'Godiva had hurried from stable to shed, and was pausing on the 'sodden ground just above the river, looking over its wind-swept surface, that was silver and black alternately— as the cloud and moon changed places. In one of these bursts of light, her eye caught sight of a dark object floating over against one side of the submerged field. It appeared to -her at first to be a long black box, but shifting her point of sight, she identified it as a coffin. It seemed much water-logged, very little of its sides being visible above the surface of the pool. Her gaze became fascinated by the thing, so strangely in character with its surroundings. How it came there her scared wits could not divine; but whilst it captured her eyes, her brain received the im- pression that a. mystery of generations was now about to be solved. And, there followed a prompt- ing. to go at once to the Rector, whose interest she was certain of ensuring.

ing. In trie-rrh;s-t—ro-c-an-" were a number of family portraits, and one of these formed the, subject of a clever speculation of the Rector's. It was the picture of a strikingly handsome woman, attired in white silk, the dress being of a curiously antique style. A great mass of golden hair tossed upon her shoulders; but the specially noteworthy feature was this—that she wore a massive chain and belt of finely-wrought. gold, the belt having a clasp inlaid with precious- stones. Little did the Rector know how near he was to the facts when he formulated and propounded this theory: "This is a portrait of Charles Latrelle's wife. She must have been ' an actress--very likely en- gaged specially to take part in the Spires revels. I can imagine the squire visiting Spires for the shows, becoming enarnoured of this woman, and beating down all obstacles, at- length bringing her home to Brampton as his wife. He loads her with favours, buys her ex- pensive clothes and costly jewellery, loves her madly, guards her jealously, neglects, everything for her; and she, unable to adapt herself to rural life, prBmaturely dies. Eccentric before, he is morbidly so now. Ile buries her in the orchard, thinking that there her remains would lie unmolested. I have no doubt this chain and belt- Cost £6OO, if a penny. The weight, the workmanship, the stones, warrant such an assumption. I feel sure there were rings in the coffin, but I could not get my fingers into a certain waistcoat pocket to re- cover them. My friends," concluded Mr. Atherstone, "the good old Bicker has saved the family fortunes!" It had. A certain noble, wealthy lady, living- in London, a great patron of the drama, had' the story from Rex, of whom she is particu- larly fond. She persisted in advancing £4OO upon the cliain and belt, which she said she. would lend to Codiva directly she could be found a part in which they could be worn. I This has already been accomplished, and this much beyond—the heirlooms have been re- f:teemed by Mr. and Mrs. Rex Litson, whose pur- pose is to steadily purchase Heron Grange of the old squire and Mrs. Latrelle, and convert it, WO' such a place of rest for a pair of artistes of supreme talent as shall make its memories and I associations an abiding joy. The young lady's name was Codiva Latrelle. Her father had been for some time dead. Of her mother we know somewhat; but she had a brother, of whom just now nobody knew any- thing. The old gentleman who occupied the arm- chair by the sunposititious fire was her grand- father, Francis Latrelle, the nominal owner of Heron Orange. They were the living representa• tives of an old Huguenot family that had settled at Spires at the time of the revocation of the edict of Nantes, over two hundred years before. As silk-weavers, they had prospered signally, so much so, that Spires to this ay is reaping the advantage of their handsome benefactions, made nit of gratitude for the asylum afforded them. Then. in an _evil hour, Gabriel Latrelle gave up the loom, and settled down upon the land in Brampton. This .was a hundred years ago, but though he brought considerable wealth with him, the fortunes -8f the house from that time steadily declined. . Rex Litsoit learnt all this and more during the following six ,or seven weeks he remained in the neighbourhood. For .if Brampton had its win- ter ghost,/ the thin, pale actor became its autumn one. As may be supposed, he very shortly brought his eye ,to ho redoctered by Mrs. Lat- relle, and established quite an acquaintanceship. In his flittings about the parish he became friendly with the Rector, who took a fancy to him, and stood a lot of pumping about Godiva Latrelle. it ba,-e-,ened that in Sentember a sale of work took place upon the itectory lawn. and Mr. ilex was eaally induced to take part in the entx!rtain- ments connected' with it. The Roy al Valades.‘^ Anycne having known 13almmel in Queea Victoria's days, would scarcely recognise the interior of the house, which, curing the past year or two has been entirely re-decorated and arranged. It. has teen said 'that Queen Alexandra has never cared much for her Highland home, but as a matter of fact her Ma;esty gteatly enjoys a spell at Balmoral, where she leads, as she does at Sandringham, the simple open- air life she loves so well. Queen Victoria always maintained a complete permanent staff of servants at each of her palaces,but their present Majesties move the whole household about with them, only leaving enough domestics to ensure the proper up-keep of each Royal residence. The " Simple Life." The crowded state of the Spas, both at home and abroad suggests that the " so-called " simple life "is more of a phrase than a reality. Dr. I Abernethy, who may be s.aid to have been the discoverer of the digestive system, recommended his patients to -live on sixpence a day—and earn it. But for every 'person eho lived the luxurious life in his time, a , hundred do so nowadays, and hence the proprietors of fashionable hotels, at all the " physic " watering places are enabled to charge their guests exhorbitant prices for the food they are told they had better not eat. No doubt it is a MOTO pleasant way of getting through life than Dr. Abernethy's, if you can afford to be ill comfortably, and that is obviously why so many who are loud in their praise of simple living,so long as it is far removed from their ORTI surroundings are found , taking the fashionable three wee L-s cure at this the ' time of the year. A Royal Soup.—The Austrian Court is famed for its elaborate Menus, the first item often being a special soup called " Olio." as was the case at the Emperor's I luncheon to King Edward the other day at the Imperial Villa at Tsai. The recipe, which was long kept secret by the chefs in the Vienna Ilofburg, is said ter be as I follows :—Take seven pounds of beef, and six pounds,' of veal,and cut into small pieces, lay side by side in a ' deep pan, and cover with a thin layer of sliced suet,' upon this again lay four onions cut into slices, and over the whole pour just one pint of wster. Then place on the stove and allow to stand for two hours. 'then half till the pen with water, and allow to boil gently, the scum being taken off continually. After two hours more add half a leg of mutton, half a bare or rabbit, two chickens, two partridges, all cut up, and besides parsley, celery roots, cabbage, turnips and carrots, all cut into slices. Then fill the pan to the brim with water, and allow to boil five hours. The soup it then put aside to cool, and after taking eff the crust of fat, is passed through a fine cullender. It can be kept for days. but no salt should be edded until the scup is sent to the table. Lord Clancaity's 117arrisee.—T1 e Earl of Clancarty whose marriage with Miss Mary Ellis is to take place in London the beginning of October, owns a very fine old family seat in Gaibally Park, near Balliusloe, Co. Galway. The park is said to be the finest in the West of Ireland, and has a private golf course laid out in its midst. The home was rebuilt in )819, and is a grey stone mansion, surrounded by beautifully wooded grounds and gardens. Lord Clancerty's first wife who died in 1906 was MISS Belle Dillon, a popular music- hall artist whom he married in 1889. She left three sons and a daughter. The eldest. Lord Eikonnel,-st hose twin brother died when three years old, will be sex en- teen next Christmas. Miss Mary Ellis was presented at one of this year's Courts, so that she is marrying in her first season, and VMS but twenty last June, being nine- teen years younger than Lord Clancaity. Bracelets for Men.—Ever since his marriage the King has worn a heavy gold bangle on his wrist, and from that time gold bangles have been donned more or less by society men. Jr.st now there is quite a revival in this direction, as there is indeed in the masculine wedding ring, which like the gold bangle usual boasts an inscription inside. All Queen Victoria's sons have worn wedding rings, and the Duke of Connaught, wears also a wide gold bracelet, which VMS a gift from the Duchess in her early married days. The New Plaids.— Quite an epidemic of plaids obtains at the moment, and taken altogether plaid costumes are a great improvement upon those of last year. In the first place, the colours of the new fabrics are softer and more artistically blerded, and then the idea of mixing , the plaids with _stripes dces away with monotony. Leading tailors are using the plaids more as a trimming' upon striped fabrics, and this in skilful hands is proving an ideal conbination. Sleeveless Coats.—The modish woman is pinning her faith to the sleeveless coat which may be quaint and artistic, but is of little use as a wrap. In shape, it, somewhat resembles the long sac, but it is slashed up under the arms, and at the back, almost to the waist, moreover it is cut away well from the neck. Dame Fashion baailecreed that over our warm woollen gowns we are to wWar coats of the above description, built of thick corded silk, heavily embroidered and braided, the colours matching those seen in the gowns. Pockets.—lt IS many years now, since we have been allowed pockets but tailors promise to be hinder to as in this direction—when coats are concerned. Dress- makers too, are allowing us little fancy pockets in our blouses, hidden away among folds, but so far is little hope of the skirt pocket appearing again. We shall have to continue to rely upon our underskirt pockets, against which little can be said save that the process of reaching them is sot altogether so graceful as one could desire. The Half-penny Postage Stamps.—Although we live in a utilitarian age, it is still considered something of a slight to write to one's friends on postcards. Even the craze for picture postcards has not altogether killed this sentimental objection which the late Mr. W. E. Gladstone did his best to eliminate by his con- stant use of the halfpenny card. But now it seems, some people object to receiving letters stamped with two halfpenny beads instead of a penny one. A good many of us n:ake it a rule to buy only halfpenny stamps, and they do equally well for card and letter postage, whereas, with only penny ones, we are some- times placed in a dilemma. But if we have correspond- ence with an old aunt, from whom we have expecta- tions, or a duchess, or other aristocratic folks, it would seem safer to use perny stamps, in case they might be touchy regarding such sentimental ideas of etiquette. . TRICKS OF THE WIND. During a great volcanic eruption in .the Hawaiian Islands, the smoke rose to a height of between five and six miles, and then drifted away to the north-east. At a distance of 609 miles it settled on the surface of the sea, and was then carried back by the north- east wind i>o its place of origin, where it ar- rived a fortnight after its original departure, and coyered the entire group of islands with its heavy pall. Some time. ago a steamer en- tered the Galita Chanhel between the island of that name/and the coast of Tunis, when a • fine dust began to darken the air, and soon afterwards to fall on deck. Some of this dust was collected, and has now been sub- jected to chemical analysis. Its constituents proved that it had been carried high in the air from the Sahara Desert, and had finally dropped into the Mediterranean.

A NEw COAT. One of the distinguishing features of the pre- sent season's modes is the great popularity of the separate coat. These coats are made in a surprising variety of shapes and materials, the latter varying from thin, light cloth to thick, soft, dull, black satin. Amongst the most fash- ionable coats are those with a suggestion of the Directoire stylo in their, cut. The smart model pictured in our sketch is distinctly Directoire in shape, and is a particularly modish and becorh- ing garment. The original was carried out ii. verw fine soft cloth of an especially attractive

shade of rather dark green. The upper part was cut in bolero fashion at the back, though the fronts had an unbroken sweep from neck to hem, and had a seam down the. middle, the two sides being cut into points, each point being adorned by a big button, and coming over the top of the pleated skirts of the coat. From the neck turned back a simple round collar of rather dull black satin, the wide cape sleeves, cut in one with the coat, being lined with similar satin. The bottom of the coat was sloped sharply from front to back, the back being considerably longer than the front.

div.head: WATCH – RtsrGS.
div.p: WATCH - RtsrGS.

The development of the watch as in article of adornmefit is an interesting little chapter in the history of the modern jewellery. Not so long ago the watch was worn by women on a long chain, a little pocket -being placed in i their dresses for its safe-keeping. Then there came thu ultra - ornamental watch, with elaborately- enamelled and richly - jewelled back, which was worn as a pendant, being fastened to the dress with a jewelled pin. The watch set in the centre of a gold bracelet followed, and then women suddenly discovered that their purse-bags offered a suitable setting for their watches. To-day, or rather to-morrow, for the new mode has just been introduced to London, the finger will have established itself, says the Daily Graphic, as the correct place for the wearing of the watch. The watch-ring is not, as might be thought, a cum- bersome ornament. In -appearance it suggests an antique marquise ring, the inner part of the marquise forming the face of a tiny watch. Though so sr all, the mechanism is perfect, and the little watch is framed in precious stones, pre- ferably diamonds. Later on we shall see it re- produced in eheaper styles, for the watch-ring is a decidedly practical little novelty.

Miss Marie Corelli has returned this season to Grantown-on-Spey, where she spent six weeks last summer. She has again taken the old-world and picturesque house called "The Garth." which belongs to Mrs. Stewart, a cousin of Sir Claud Macdonald. Her admiration for Strath- spey was expressed in a recent letter to one of the tOwnspeople: "I most heartily wish Gran- town and its pleasant people every success in their loyal efforts to maintain the charm and at- tractiveness of a Highland resort which, to my thinking,. is one of the most beautiful places in the world." ,

div.head: TO-DAY'S RECII7.
div.p: TO-DAY'S RECII7.

PEAR TART.—Every Englishman and woman Knows the charms of apple tart, but very few people are aware, say= a contemporary, that pears, properly treated beforehand, make an even better tart than apples. Select ripe, but not over-ripe, mellow pears; peel them very thinly. Core and halve them, and place in a clean fireproof china dish. Duet them thickly with sifted sugar. Add a little finely-grated lemon zest, and enough water barely to cover the pears. Stew gently until thoroaghly cooked, then leave till cold. When cold. Dour over the pears the contents of a bd. jug of cream, cover with a good short crust. and bake in the usual way. Serve hot or cold. If preferred, puff paste may be used instead of short paste.. but for children the latter is better. Cloves may also be Used in place of the lemon zest, if liked.

ANTS AS WEATHER PROPHETS.

A correspondent of Science Siftings writes to say that from observations he has con- ducted, the ant proves tin . excellent weather prophet. "When you go out on a spring, morning," we are told, "and find the ants busily engaged in clearing out their nests and dragging the sand and bits of earth to the surface, you may be sure that no matter how cloudy it is; there will be no rain that day, and the probabilities are for several days of good weather. On the other hand, if you see the ants about the middle of a spring or summer afternoon hurrying back to the nest, and a sentinel trotting round in every direction, looking up stragglers and urging them to gat home as soon as they can get there, you may figure on a rain that after- noon or night. When the last of the wan- derers is found, the picket hurries in and the neat is securely sealed from the inside, to keep out the water. It is very seldom that ants are taken by surprise by the approach of a shower.

div.head: ELECTRICITY, HEAT, AND ETHER.
div.p: ELECTRICITY, HEAT, AND ETHER.

Professor- Frederick Hovenden has chal- lenged the greatest scientists of the world to disprove his statement that electricity, heat, and ether are the same thing—a fluid which, if properly illuminated, is visible to the naked eye. •"Ether," says Professor Hoven- den, "is a fluid which permeates everything. It is omnipresent. It regulates the smallest chemical alteration. Consequently it regu- lates the largest and most complicated alte- ration. Hence it regulates life. It is, there- fore, omnipotent." Professor Hovenden, fu thermore, says: "Every organic being is governed by the flow of ethet. Every haman being was formed by the same means as the chicken was formed, and when this is under- stood a new order of thought will arise which will add materially to the happiness of man- kind. It is a sublime idea that every one of the millions of forms we find in Nature is re- gulated by this subtle force, this ether or spirit, omnipresent And omnipotent—a power without which animal and vegetable life would cease to exist, without which there would be no water and no fire, and all would be frozen."

div.head: VARIABLE LATITUDE.
div.p: VARIABLE LATITUDE.

Among the most important researches which astronomers have in hand is an in- vestigation of that period of minute osciLlan tion of the earth's axis, whith gives rise to the phenomena of variable latitude. Upon co-ordinating several hundred Indian Ocean determinations with corresponding results of the Berlin Observatory, Professor Foer- ster, of Berlin, finds that beyond doubt the latitude in Berlin during the period in- creased by one-third of a second, and in- creased in the Indian Ocean by exactly the same amount. As long ago as 1876 it had been put forth that irregular motions of the earth's axis to the extent of half a second may be produced by the

TEMPOHARY CHANGES OP SEA LEVEL, due to meteorological causes. Professor Focr- ster points out the need of four permanent stations for regular and continued observa- tions of this change in latitude, mid so to de- termine the causes of those variations, which have hitherto been put down to irregularities in observations. Not only is the research of the first importance in respect to the funda- mental observational work in astronomy, but it has exceeding interest in connection with tidal, meteorological, and geological observa- tions and speculations.

div.head: MARINER'S COMPASS.
div.p: THE MARINER'S COMPASS.

Nothing in the navigational equipment of a ship has been the subject of more anxious scientific research or receives more jealous care than the mariner's compass, says Mr. Frank T. Bulieu in the !Vimlsar Magazine. The popular notion of the compass needle al- ways pointing north and south is—well, more inaccurate than even popular notions usually are. Even under the most favourable condi- tions, there are only certain places on the surface of the earth where the compass needle does point north and south, and it is quite safe to say that such conditions are never found on board any ship. But we must go further and say that no more unfavourable position could be found for a compass than on board a modern Pteamship, which is a complicated mass of steel, all

TENDING TO DRAW THE COMPASS NEEDLE from its allegiance to the magnetic pole of the earth," warring influences which must needs be counteracted by all sorts of devices which hedge round the instrument by an in- visible wall of conflicting currents of magnet- ism. And as if this were not enough, there are now huge dynamos to he reckoned With, producing electric currents for all sorts of purposes on board. In the midst of these mystic currents the poor little compass needle, on which the mariner. depends for his guide across the trackless deep, hangs suspended like one shrinking saint sur. rounded by legions of devils.

div.head: NUMBER SEVEN.
div.p: THE NUMBER SEVEN.

Among all the numbers, none other- seems to have attained the qlebrity of 7. There are seven days in the week, seven years of plenty, seven years o-f famine, seven wise men of Greece, seven wonders of the world, seven Mohammedan heavens. seven notes in the musical scale, seven colours in the solar spec- trum, &c. The visible moving bodies of the heavens- are seven—sun, moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, The Great Bear consists of seven principal stars; the Pleiades were seven sisters, the seventh hav- ing concealed herself, which accounts- for but six stars being visible. Now there is quite a wonderful array which may be derived from the number 7. Upon attempting to convert the fraction 17 into a decimal, we shall find it impossible to complete-the operation. We obtain, however, a recurring series of num- bers, thus:
• 1-7 =•14571428571428.57 -F . This .is a circulating decimal. Suppose, now, we write the series of figures thus obtained :

Multiplying by 1 we, of course,/ reproduce the number, but multiplying by 2, we obtain 285714. This product is composed of pre- cisely the same figures, And ..not only that, but the figures are arranged in the same order. Multiplying j.vy 3, we get 428571; again the same fieures and in the came order. Mul- tiplying succsesstvety hy 4,5, and 6, we get 571428,- 714285. and 857142, possessing tho same properties These results may be made more strikisig, perhaps, by arranging tho figure in a circlet _

div.head: INDEPENDENT ORDER OF RECRUITER.
div.p: INDEPENDENT ORDER OF RECRUITER.
Warrington District No. 4.

The half-yearly meeting of the above District was held in the Brunswick-road Mission Hall, Earlestown on Saturday last. Bro. Joseph Hill, D.C.R., presided, and called the Council to Order at 3 p.m. there being a good attend- ance of officers and representatives present.

WIGAN DISASTER. The ordinary routine of the business was suspended in order that Bro. E. Walkden, of Ashton, District Trustee, should move a resolution of sympathy with the friends and relatives who have so seriously suffered in the Mining disaster at Abram, near Wigan. Bro. James Shaw, Warrington, District Trustee, seconded, the resolution being carried silently. Bro. W. Wright, Warrington moved, and Bro. C. S. Fellow, Warrington, seconded that a grant of £lO be sent from the District special fund, to the distress fund opened by the Mayor of Wigan to relieve the suffering and distress occasioned by the sad disaster. The minutes of the previous meeting were read and confirmed. Several notices of motion from the tents were dealt with. The report of the Juvenile District was given by Bro. W. Baxendale, which showed that the juvenile work continued to make satisfactory progress. The Executive's and District Secretary's reports were given, and being considered satisfactory were adopted. An invitation from the representative of Charity tent was given for the next District meeting to be held in Warrington, and also an invitation from the repre- sentative of Providence tent, Latchford. The invitation from Charity tent was accepted. ' Ten was splendidly arranged for the officers, repre- sentatives and friends in the Mission Hall. After a tea a vote of thanks was tendered to the friends of Mizpah tent Earlestown, for their hospitality, seconded by Bro. H. 13rereton and ably supported by a vigorobs and humorous speech from Bro. R. Harrison, Garswood. Bro. Dring, suitably responded to the vote of thanks on behalf of the members of Mizpah tent and wished the District continued success and prosperity.

div.head: AMERICAN BEAUTY.
div.p: AMERICAN BEAUTY.

Apparently there is something propitious in the Christian name of Maude or Maud. • For as in England we have had to confess ourselves charmed by the grace and artistry of Miss Maud Allan, in America susceptible hearts have been captivated by the beauty of Miss _Maude Adams. Hers is a type of loveliness very different from the average stage favourite's and her sweet disposition and quiet unpretentious ways may clearly be inferred from the photograph reproduced above. Miss Adams has appeared with phenomenal 'success in New York in an English version of "Les Bouffons," a play which was originally produced by Madame Sarah Bernhardt in France. When this production is ended, Mr. Charles Frohman has made arrangements for her to visit England where no doubt she will extend her conquests. She made a brief appearance in London a few years ago.

div.head: Mulai-Hafid.
div.p: Mulai-Hafid.
Abd-el-Aziz.
THE OLD SULTAN OF MOROCCO AND THE NEW.

After years of impossible restlessness and mismanagement in the North African Empire, .the Sultan, Abdul Aziz, has been routed in battle with the pretender, his brother, Mulai Hafid. The fight -occurred at a little place called Ben Grir, about fifty miles from Marrakesh. the southern capital. The Azizites were taken completely by surprise, and it is said that after a few shots had been fired, most of the Sultan's troops sided with Mulai Hafid. The deposition of Abdul may place France in a difficult position, for she has steadily supported hina and refused to recognise the rival. Mulai Hafid's victory makes him by Moorish law and custom the only Sultan of Morocco de jure, and, as such, apparently he will have to be recognised by the Powers. Abdul Aziz is said to intend to go to Damascus, where he will -remain until conditions are favourable for return to Morocco.

The Examiner Saturday, August 29, 1908.
TALKS FOR A QUIET HOUR.
SWEET POISON.
BY REV. C. SILVESTER HORNE, M.A.

One of the discoveries which our city chil- dren make when we send them into the coun- try is that the country-side is full of poisons. Motherly souls who look after them give them frequent affectionate warnings on this subject. They koow well the force of that instinct which tempts every wall-constructed child to test the merit of every flower and berry by applying its teeth to it. There seems to be no reason to the ordinary boy or girl why the sweet earth should give birth to the wholesome corn and the baleful poppy side by side; still less why the poppy should look so much more brilliant and attractive than the wheat. How did the poison get into the poppy, and why did it get there? Why did not God make a world without poisons? Or, if it was necessary to make them, why did He dress them up 60 prettily and smartly, and give them such an appeal to the eye? Ought they not by a prudent Providence to be marked for what they are, and endowed with a sinister and forbidding appearance, so that children would run away from them instead of reaching out innocent infant hands to clutch them and to taste them?

The berries of yew or nightshade—how tempting they appear! Even Mother Eve's apple could not have looked more friendly to her eyes than these jolly berries to the eyes of children who know nothing of the perils as well as the charms of the garden of the world. Centuries ago a wise writer warned his fellow-men against looking at the wine when it Wee red.' He saw the seductive light that gleamed and burnt in the wine and tempted men and women to their undoing. This was what John Milton wrote of as "the charmed cup of Circe." The peril is exactly that charm in the cup. It has lurked smiling there, and sparkling: Since Bacchus first from out the purple grape Crushed the sweet poison of misused.wine. Sweet poison! There is little or no danger in the poison that is bitter and ugly to taste and sight. The danger is in the sweetness, the lusciousness, the brilliance.

I' am reminded of all this because of my neighbourhood to a famous spot, beautiful in itself, and glorious even in decay by reason of notable memories. There are few fairer soenes than the ruins of old Ludlow Castle, the seat of kings and princes, and remask- able for association with men greater than the kings who patronised it—with Philip Sidney, and Richard Baxter, and Samuel Butler, and John Milton. The link between Milton and Ludlow is perhaps the most romantic, as it is certainly the most precious of all. If the Visitor of to-day stands upon the keep and looks away southwards to the wooded country he may easily figure to him- self the days when all around this mighty fortress lay a vast forest. And if he loves the storied and fabled past, he may like to picture to himself the three young children of the Earl of Bridgewater on their way to Ludlow Castle lost in the forest; and then the alarm of the parents, and the fitting out of the rescue parties, and, finally, the triumphant escort of the discovered boys and girl_ to the great friendly stronghold where their parents ruled in state.

Then appears upon the some that fine genius, the yowl..''. John Milton, barely of age, but with the fair, oval face which a Court artist had already immortalised because of its rare beauty. Around this simple incident of the lost children he throws the magic of his fantasy, and lo! the green forest is peopled by the weird enchanter Comus and his rabble crew, who have drunk his potions, and lost the endowments of humanity. There he lives, to seduce the innocent with fair and specious words and the "sweet poisons " which he brews; and there is the appointed theatre where the pitched battle between Vice and Virtue is decided in the persons of Comus and the Virtuous Maiden who, in the simplicity of her trust in God, defied him to do her injury. We all know how, within the decaying but still stately walls of the old Banqueting Hall at Ludlow, John Milton's Masque of Comus was performed, and the girl "Alice," the heroine of the adventure in the forest, represented the lady in her mystic ordeal against the temptations of Comus. No more sublime affirmation of the power of innocence has ever been made than was first uttered in the hearing of the splendid court of Ludlow Castle on the night of September 29th, 1634. - _

John Milton had always an extraordinarily penetrating knowledge of evil, and wherein its fascination consists. Whenever he Ale- scribed it he made it really beautiful. The power of evil in the world, as he saw, is not that it is ugly and hateful; but that it is brilliant and lovely. The daring of his de- scriptions in "Paradise Lost!' of the fallen Spirit is notorious: High on a throne of royal state, which far Outshone the wealth of Ormuz or of Ind, Or whore the gorgeous East with lavish hand Showers on her sons barbaric pearl and gold, Satan exalted sat. That is the picture of evil as Milton saw it: throned in royal state, outshining in splen- dour the wealth of the Orient, made fascinat- ing to the Faze with magnificence of pearl and gold. It 16 on rrudacious picture, but it is true to life. Nobody has ever seen and felt the power of evil who does not know what John Milton knew.

*.* So it came to pass that the fatal magician who exercises his spells upon the lady in "Collins " appears as a gentle Shepherd, in guileless Ritstoral fashion: • Offering to every weary traveller His orient liquor in a crystal glass. All is attractive, and speaks of refreshment. What wrong can possibly lurk in such a glass? When Comus presents his cup to the lady we are given to understand that there is addi- tional attraction in the sparkle and beauty of that which it contains: Behold this cordial julep here That flames and dances in his crystal hounds. The "flame" and the "dance" •of the "orient liquor in a crystal,glass" are the ex- pression of John Milton's sense of the bril- liant form, the beauty, and the glory in which many of our most seductive temptations make their appeal to us. In the Masque the cup remains untasted because the will of Virtue remains steadfast to reject what the noble in- stinct of Innocence reveals to be deadly. But surely as the ladies and gentlemen assembled in gallant fashion in the Banqueting Hall at Ludlow Castle on that historic September night, and listened to John Milton's play, they cannot have failed to learn his lesson. Life is by no means all plain sailing. God does not label the products of nature, though He does supply us with instincts, and the faculties by which we may turn experiences to account. We thread our way at times through dark and threatening shades.

In moments of exhaustion and extremity there are presented to us opportunities ' that we know to be lo W and false and mean, but that promise at least some ease and comfort. The young fellow whose health i almost un- dermined by hard work in a position of little promise is suddenly offered a place of larger dignity and remuneration, but where con- science must abdicate her seat. He knows that it is the cup of Counts, offered to him just when he is exliTisted in the dark wood, and can see no daylight anywhere. The prospect is of ease and pleasure and the soft, sweet life of luxury. Alas! he yields. But the poison is there none the less, and is soon fatally at work in his system. The fruits of the tree of dea,th have more of colour upon them than the plain fruits of the tree of life. But the or 4 fruit has in it the mysterious taint that destroys gradually the sensitiveness of the soul and so works desolation and de- struction. After all, we have to learn to discriminate between the good and the evil; and it belongs to the very alphabet of educa- Coy that things are not what they 09enat

NUMEROUS WARRINGTON SUGGESSES.

The result lists of the recent Oxford Local Examina- tions were issued by the secretary of the delegacy on I Monday morning and showed that candidates from !Warrington and district had acquitted themselves very creditably. The total number of candidates examined was 21,155, namely 3,526 preliminary, 8,302 junior, and 9,557 senior. Of these, 2,831 preliminary, 0,007 junior, and 0,331 senior passed, making a total of 15,169. The I total number of candidates and other persons entered for the examination was 21,533, of whom 318 failed to present themselves for examination. The number of senior candidates offering themselves for examination shows an increase over last year of nearly 50 per cent. This large growth appears to be due to various independent causes. The practice of sending in picked boys or girls from a given school is giving place to that of entering whole classes or forms, besides which many candidates announced their desire to qualify for admission to a training college for elementary teachers, or for exemption from a university or professional examination. It is also satisfactory to note that there is aconsiderable increase in the percentage of successful senior boy candidates. There is a tie for the first place in the first class of the seniors, in which there were 179 candidates against 95 last year, A. A. C. Burton, Hitchin Grammar School (principal, Mr. J King), and E. A. Ifelsham, Mount St. Mary's College, Chesterfield (principal, Rev. L. P. Wolfe), being bracketed equal. There was a slight decrease in the number of junior candidates presenting themselves for examination. The number who succeeded in obtaining a first-class was 253 compared with 200 last year. The first place is gained by L. P. L. Edwards,Whitgift Grammar Sclaool,Croydon (principal, Mr. S. 0. Andrew). The scholarship of £lO offered by the delegates to the boy placed highest in the honours list is awarded to L. P. L. Edwards ; and a similar scholarship for a girl candidate is given to K. W. Smith, Culcheth Hall, Bowdon. The number of preliminary gindidates also shows a slight decrease ; 41 of these are placed in the first class as against 51 last year. The first place is gained by S. F. Grace, St. Francis Xavier's College, Liverpool (principal, Rev. J. Browne). This year, of the senior candidates, 38 girls were i placed n the first class, 99 in the second, and 472 in the third ; of the juniors, 55 girls were placed in the first class, 86 in the second, and 368 in the third ; of the preliminary. 7 girls were placed in the first class, 13 in the second, and 109 in the third. div.head: OUR LOCAL GiIURGE3.
div.p: OUR LOCAL GiIURGE3.
"Sankey anti His Songs."

IThe Rev. R. H. Letheren preached an interesting and powerful sermon at Golbarne-street Baptist Church, on Sunday evening on "Sankey and his Sangs." There was a large congregation and daring the service SJ:II3 of Sankey's hymns were sung. Annanncing as his text Ezekiel xxxiii. 32 " And la thou art unto them as a I very lovely song of one that hath a pleasant voice and can play well on an instreruent," Mr. Letheren said he read those words as a motto for what he wished to say about a man who could play well on many instru- ments, and who hsd a voice more than pleasant and Iwhose memory would be kept green for many genera- tions by the lovely songs with which his name was linked—lra David Sankey who on Friday August 11th passed away at his home in Brooklyn at the age of 88. No apology was needed for making the story of Mr. Sankey the subject of a Sunday evening service. Though he was not precisely the pioneer of that widely extended use of sacred song in the service of the Evangel, his was the best known name in that connection. Such signal service as be rendered to the Church at large was worthy of recognition and remembrance. He could touch on only a few points of Sankey's unique life and those points would make their own appeal. And first he would call attention to the intimate relationship between salvation and song. The first song lof Israel celebrated their salvation out of Egypt. Tao song book of the Jewish Church still serves to express the heart's experience whether of joy or sorrow. Songs heralded Christ's own birth, and His birth in the soul made it a nest of singing birds. It was the genius of the Gospel that it could be set to sang. lie much doubted whether the philosophy of Spencer or of Schopenhauer would lend itself to lyrics. A man's religion had not done ranch for him if it had not at least taught him to make a joyful noise to the God of his salvation. Every genuine revival of religion was associated with a revival of sacred song. And when two unknown Americans came to England in 1873 and were the means of a great religions awakening, with Moody the evangelist appeared Sankey the singer. An account of Sankey's boyhood up to the time of his joining the Church at the age of 15 led Mr. Letherea to remark that the " sons of the Tabernacle " had been amongst the greatest contributors to the world's welfare. A reference to the well-known meeting between Stanley and Livingstone introduced a descrip- tion of the first meeting between Moody and Sankey, and that partnership that became a romance ef evangelism was characterized as a union of sweetness and strength that went victoriously through the world. The order of the two names suggested the exquisite per- fection with which Sankey played "second fl idle." Mr. Letheren quoted Dr. G. A. Smith's estimate of the Great Mission 25 years afterwards, show- ing how .it quickened social reform as well as individual religion, and that Senkey's share ,in it was scarcely seoond to that of Moody. The ' preacher then sketched the man at the American organ, and spoke of the qualities that belonged to his singing and told the stories of some of his best-known songs. The Hymn Book known as " Sankey's " was compiled ,as the outcome of that mission and the popularity of the hymns was witnessed by their being sung by Anglicans and Nonconformists, by missionaries in China, India and Africa, in the forests of Uganda and lin tiny cabins of fiThing smacks on the North Sea. Later visits of MeSankey to England in the eighties and in Two were referred to and then an account was given lof the last public service of praise he conducted in 1902 when he led the children in " Blest be the 'tie that binds." Rev. John Wilson of 'Woolwich saw him last year and brought the message " I'm just ' waiting by the river for the summons and living in the 23rd Psalm." He sang "There'll he no dark valley when Jesus comes" and said it was probably the last time he would ever sing. He ordered the words" Gad ' is love" to be cut upon his tomb that future generations might know the faith in which he died.

div.head: SINGING DOWN THE HORN.
div.p: SINGING DOWN THE HORN.

It is an art to sing, as everyone knows. It is more of an art to sing acceptably into talking machine records. The process is fall of fascination and interest both to the artiste and the public. And to both there is considerable mystery about it, for the manufacturers jealously guard their secret processes. The singer is placed before the large end of a trumpet, the small end reaching within a curtained enclosure where the record- ing export is busily engaged in looking after the intricacies of his part of the work. It makes artistes nervous at first, this singing before a hole in the wall. There is an uncanniness about it to which they are peculiarly succeptibly. They miss the brace that comes from facing a sympathetic audience. Yet artistes who sing down the horn sing to vastly larger audiences than to those that see them in the flesh. Especially is this true of the singers who make Columbia Records. Columbia Records have an immense circulation and many a singer's voice is beard in continents on which he never set foot, and beside seas that de never visited. Columbia Records fit any talking machine, and make it sound better than ever before. Some of the newest titles are" My dreams " by John Eardsley, " Sae, Sue, Sue" by George H. Elliott, "Selections from 'Havana'" by the Royal Regimental Band. Hear them and ' other titles at your dealer's. He will be glad to play them for you. A copy of the latest list will be sent on receipt of postcard request to Columbia Phonograph Company, 64 and 66, Oxford-street, London, W.

Tat is avEa—t it royal natural kogs of earth. The grass grows right damm to the water at , beach, and within fifty feet of the everlasting 533. Toe trees also gre:v down to the salty edge of thing and one sits in their shade an 3 looks seaward ftt a majestic surf thundering in on the beach to one's very I feet. Half a mile out, where is the reef, the white- , headol combers thrust suddenly skyward out as the placid term aise-blue and come rolling in to share. Ono after another they came, a mile lanz,, with smoking crests, the white battalions of the infinite army of the sea. And 033 sits and listens to the perpetual roar, and watches the unending procession, an-f fools tiny and fragile before this treuenicus form expressing itself in fury and foam an I sound. Inieet one feels micro- scopically small, and the thought that one may wrestle with this sea raises in one's imagination a thrill of appreheasion,.almost of fear. _

And sudimily, out there where a big smoker lifts s'ayivard, rising like a sea god from out of the welter of spume and chinning white, on the giddy, toppling, overhanging, and downfalling, precarious crest appears the d irk head of ain in. Swiftly he rises thronah the rashing white. His black shoulders, his chest, his loins, his liaahs —all is abraptly projected on one's vision. Where but the moment befora was only the ocean's desolation ant invincible roar is now a man, erect, full- stature& not struggling frantically in that wild move- ment, not buried and crushed and buffeted by those mighty monsters, but stanliy; above them all, calm and superb, poisel on the giddy summit, his feet buried in the churning foam, the salt smoke rising to his knees, and all the rest of him in the free air and flashing sunlight, and he is flying through the air: flying forward, flying fast as the surge on which he stands fie is a Meroury---a blank Mercury. His heels kre winged, and in them is the swiftness of the sea. In truth, from out of the sea ho has leaped upon the back of the Sal, and he is riding the sea that roars and bellows and cannot shake him from its back. But no frantic out-reaching nod balancing is his Ho is impassive, motionless as a statue carved suddenly by some miracle out of the sea's depth from which he rose. And straight on toward shore he flies on his winged heels and the white crest of the breaker. There is a wild burst of foam, a long, turrrultnous, rushing sound as the breaker falls futile and spent on the beach before you; and there at your feet, calmly steps ashore a Kanaka, burnt black by the tropic sun. Several minutes ago he was speck a quarter of a mile away. Ile has "bitted the bull-mouthed breaker " and ridden it in, and the pride in the feat shows in the carriage of his magnificent body as ho glances for a moment carelessly at you who sit in the shade of the shore. lie is a fianaka—and more, he is a man a natural king, a member of the kingly species that LAS mastered matter and the brntes and larded it over creation.—We quote from an article by Jack Londou iri the Septe tabor " Pall Mall Magazine," in the course of which the author gives simple directions for the practice of what he calls this " royal sport." CURIOUS GUIDE-POSTS. _

Tne -!alaia-zin-e-U-Oatains a very interesting article on "Itoliday making on Old Roads " accompanied by many illustration. The writer says "C taching roads show SIM 3 stages in the evoiution of the King's highway. Here and there is a relic, in the form of a mounting-block, of the days when ladies rode a-pillion, and when the state of the roads was such that nearly everybody was obliged to travel on horse- back. Chamberlayns. writing in 1619, says : There is of late such an admirable commodiousness, both for risen and women, to travel from London to the principal towns of the country that the like bath not been known in the world, and that is by stage coaches, wherein any one may be transported to any place sheltered from foul weather and foul ways, free from endamaging one's health and one's body by hard-jogging or over-violent emotions on horseback, and this not only at the low price of one shilling for every five miles, but such velocity and speed in one hour as the foreign post can make but in one day.' The average velocity and speed' was five miles per hour. Ten years after Charaberlayne wrote, however, Thomas Wright, of Warden, set up a mounting-block on the Banbury- Dtiventry road, and there it has remained ever since. Dated 1659, it is still in good condition. "There remain, too, a few, and only a few, of the early travellers' guides,most of which are on roads now deserted. A unique handing-post' on Broadway Hill points the way To Gloster. 'To Wester,' and other places, as it has pointed it for more than two centuries. Another curious guidepost is on an old and now for- saken coaching road, near Skipton •, yet another is The Pillar; a post eight feet high standing on a Roman road leading from Hope to the Snake, that emphatic highway from Glossop to Sheffield, which rises 1,061 feet above sea-level; and there is a venerable. looking example—it is, as a fact, dated 1705—at Hopton in Derbyshire." The September Windsor Magazine is a notable second Holiday Number, showing no falling off in value and variety from the recent August issue. Here is a number rich in complete stories by distinguished novelists and articles instructive and entertaining, and in both departments it is finely illustrated. In place of I the usual serial there is a story of powerful interest complete in the one issue by Eden Phillpotts, a new romantic theme by Justus Miles Forman, and other complete stories by Barry Pain, Keble Howard, Frances Rivers, Frank Richardson, Reginald Turner, Constance Cotterell and P. G. Wodehouse. Charles G. D. Roberts contributes another of his picturesque articles on animal life, and for the dog lover no fewer than twenty two of Maud Earl's admirable paintings and studies are reproduced, with a biographical aoconot of the artist's career. A timely article is supplied by Welter Camp, the Arnerisan author athlete, under the title "What America spends on College Athletics."
TABLE-TALK OF THE-DUKE OF WELLINGTON.

The Duke said," The French have no enthusiasm for anyone; there is no one." Talking of Lord Nelson, the Duke said that they had met once. He was at the Admiralty, and in the waiting-room when Nelson came in—" a man of about my own size." Lord Wilton asked," Does that print give a cnrrect likeness, accord- ing to your Grace's impression ? " The Duke, looking at it (a full-length) : "Yes ; about my own height." Lord W. said, "I remember hearing you say that he , talked only of himself." Duke : "Well, and so he did. It was all about himself; what be did in the West Indies ; he had just come from the West Indies." Lord W. said "Your Grace met Soult once in France?" "Oh, yes ; so they told me. I was fast asleep in the carriage, Ind my servant said that Soult looked in ; and I dare say he said, Oh, he's asleep, d—n him!' and turned away." This was after Toulouse. Talking of the generals assembled at Paris in 1814, when the various Austrian and Prussian generals who had been beaten by Napoleon came crowding round the Duke and expressing lots of compliments to him for having never been beaten by the Prench,the Duke pleased them immensely by saying." Ah, but you know I never met Bonaparte, and I Rave always looked on him as being as good as forty thousand men." There was an extraordinary Frenchman invited to meet the Duke at Madame de Sled's after Waterloo. The Abb4 de Pradt—a great intriguer in politics. Po he came up to the Duke and began a long speech about Napoleon—his enormous power, great talents, S:c., and the Duke, waiting for the end, feeling sure that it was to be the usual compliment to him, when to, his unutterable relief the Abb4 ended by saying, "Eh hien, de grand Colossus--h proSsent emprisonn4 dans une petite lie—ce grand travail rl l'ouvrage d'un sell! hornme—et, Monsieur le GESndral. cet Homme c'est Moi."—From "‘ The Duke ' " in the" Cornhill Magazine" for September.

NEW TURBINE STEAMER FOR THE HOOK OF HOLLAND SERVICE.—Another turbine steamer intended for the Great Eastern Railway Company's Harwich- Hook of Holland service, sister vessel to the Copen- hagen, has been launched at Messrs. Brown and Co.'s yard, Clydebank, Scotland. The ceremony was performed by Miss Lawson, daughter of Sir Arthur Tredold Lawson, Bart., director of the Great Eastern Railway Company, who named the vessel Munich. The new boat will be fitted with wire- less telegraphy and will have all the modern improve- ments in respect to heating, ventilation and lighting. The vessel which is 343 feet long, 43 feet broad, will have a speed of 20 knots per hour, and accommodation for over 200 llrst-class passengers. With the exception of a few the cabins will contain two berths only. The Munich is expected to he completed and placed on the service before the end of ths Ter,

When Mr. LLOYD-GEORGE WHAT PROTEC- was in Germany he heard TION REALLY everywhere the same story „DOES. of a rise in the price of commodities. Twenty years ago Germany was one of the cheapest countries in Europe, in the opinion of its own people, and now it is one of the dearest. Rents are higher than in this country, and wages are lower. There are those to whom these statements will appear to be disputable. The Tariff Reform League had some sort of responsibility in connection with a deputa- tion which reported that in general the German working man is much better off than the English workman. Which of these state- ments, it .may be asked, are we to believe ? Well suppose we believe neither of them for the time being ; but inquire into the facts. These are supplied at a most timely moment by the British Consul in Pomerania, The Prussian civil servants, who make up a large proportion of the population, are begging for increases of salary on the ground of the rise in the price of commodities, and they have drawn up a table showing the increased cost of the separate articles of domestic consumption. This has been sent over by the British consul in Pomerania, who I says it " speaks a very plain and impressive language," as undoubtedly it does. This price- list will at once decide the question of whether Mr. LLOYD-GEORGE or the Tariff Reforria League delegation is to be believed. The figures drawn up by the Prussian Civil Servants for the instruction of their Government do not go back to the time, twenty yeers ago, when Germany was one of the cheapest countries in Europe. They deal with the change in prices since 1896. They are based, therefore, on a com- parison with previous Protectionist rates—on prices, that is to say, under what was only a less 'severe and complete form of Protection. We take a few samples of what has happened. Linen underwear has gone up 33i- per cent. Broadly, what cost three shillings before costs four shillings now. Woollen goods have gone up by more than 60 per cent.: boots coat more by 10 to 15 per cent.; even hair- cutting charges have gone up by 50 per cent. Coming to food, it seems that meat has gone up

19 per cent.; butter, '..13 to 33 per cent.; potatoes, 20 per cent.; eggs, 22 per cent.; peas, 27 per cent.; and lentils, 85 per cent. These are merely figures which illustrate the argument, as Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN says. They might be extended over every article of domestic use and consumption. Coals are 15 per Cent. higher in summer and 22 per cent. higher in winter; all household goods are higher by from 15 to 20 per cent. ; servants and charwomen are much dearer than they were, and the washing bill has gone up by from 40 to 60 per cent. These are facts that are not marshalled for the purpose of refuting Tariff Reform figures. They are statements made by German officials, who are anxious for an increase of wages, and who are probably, or at least possibly, very strong Protectionists. Merely to sat them forth is, of course, to dispose decisively of the question of whether Mr. LLorn-G-nonon and all independent authorities, by the way— or the Tariff Reform League delegation, is most entitled to credit for veracity in connection withl the present conditions of life in Germany. That matter need not, in fact, be debated any further. That ages are lower in Germany than among ourselves is aumitted, we believe, by everybody but Tariff Reformers. They are being driven upwards in some directions, as must necessarily be the case where the cost of living increases by lea pa and bounds, unless they are, in spite of working hard, to get nearer and nearer to the starve tion limit. But the increase in wages bears no reasonable proportion to the increase in the cost of commodities. It may be higher in the case of some individual articles, and lower in the case of others ; but, as a percentage, it only counts once; whereas all the other percentages of increase are piled up on each other. But if the working classes in Germany are suffering from high prices, why do they not revolt against Pro- tection ? The answer is, in part, that they may not attribute high prices to the real cause ; and, in greater part, that Protection raises up all manner of vested interests, which would fight to the death for special privileges, an I that will c tinue to be a burden until they bocome wholly intolerable.

The Maypole Colliery dis- HELP FOR THE aster near Wigan sent a HELPLESS. thrill of horror through the country—a sensation which has since been succeeded by that of pity for the widowed and fatherless. Notwith- standing the hard times, money has simply rolled in to swell the Mayor of Wigan's fund, which yesterday reached £6,632 163. sd. This is less than half the amount really required to adequately minister to the needs of the 44 widows and 100 dependent children, while in addition there are 1,100 men out of work, with 4,000 women and children dependent upon them. It will, we have no doubt, give satisfaction locally that the Mayor has opened a shilling fund,which will enable the humblest Warrington sympathiser to contribute his mite. Already some £42 have been raised. Warrington must find at least £lOO to do justice to the sorrowful demands of its neighbour, and we have no doubt that the sum will be forth- coming before the list closes.

The vexed question of the MEDICAL INSPECTION medical inspection of Sellool OF SCHOOL children is apparently settled CHILDREN. at last. Details have been • arranged and agreed upon between the Town Clerk, the Medical Officer of Health, and the Director of Education and we I presume they will meet with the approval of the Town Council and the Education Committee at their respective meetings next week. The arrange- ments made will be found set out in detail under the heading "Town Council Business " on another page. Roughly they are as follows. The Assistant Medical Officer will devote the bulk of his time to the inspection of school children,and will apparently not touch the general infectious disease work of the town. This is, we suppose, a conces- sion to the sentiment which is alleged to be deeply embedded in the breast of every parent. Ttleir anxieties as to the Medical Officer transferring disease germs to the tender offspring who are about to enter or leave school should therefore be laid at rest. A Medical Inspection Committee will be responsible for dealinz with cases reported on by the School Medical Officer, and this Committee will also provide the necessary clerical assistance, weighing machines and other apparatus. The children will be examined at school, so that with medical inspection religious instruction, and lastly the teaching of the "three r's," the elementary day school will appear a formidable institution to the minds of the rising generation.

Those who wish to have Bon OUGH FINANCE. some information as to how the ratepayers' money is spent cannot do better than study the Borough Treasurer's annual abstract of accounts which is summarised in another column. While presenting few features out of the ordinary, it contains a mass of detail which the thoughtful townsman will no cLubt find roost interesting. The first fact of importance is contained in the aggregate balance statement which shows that the town's assets exceed the liabilities by £481,563 193, 101(1.—a comforting reflection. What will appeal most to the average reader are the returns from the various Corporation depart- ments. For instance we find that the Manchester Ship Canal litigation—now, we hope, a thing of the past—has cost the town during the year 21,49365. 63. There have been some extensive purchases of land and property, the amounts under this head including £3,537 10s. in respect of Buttermarket-street, and £4,125 153. in respect of Knutsford-road. These costs will, of course, be spread Over a number of years, the money being raised on loan. Education continues to be a very costly item, but under the new conditions we suppose it is inevitable and the ratepayer can only" grin and bear it." The accounts for the baths department disclose the fact that during the year the baths"rnade"a loss 01142303. Bd.—but in the interests of cleanliness and the public health few will be disposed to grudge the outlay. The upkeep of the bowling green at Victoria Park has cost £l4 133. 103. and the caretakers' wages absorb £67 6.3. There is a slight falling off in the receipts from bowlers-245 us. 63. as compared with £54 103. last year—but the green is obviously fulfilling a most useful purpose and we hope before long to see it followed by others in different parts of the town. The markets have brought in the handsome profit of ;£3,429 55,, while the gas department was again a splendid source of revenue, the rates benefiting to the extent of £ll,OOO after the payment of £B,OOO for annuities, interest and sinking fund. The Electricity Department, as our readers will recollect, took the unusual but generous course of contributing £2,000 to the improvement rate, to mitigate the burden on the ratepayers, and as a consequence there was only £213 to place to the reserve fund. The tramways are making good headway, the net profit being £2,580 as compared with £1,310 last year, and the whole of this sum has bean transferred to the reserve fund.

The prohibition inserted in I At OLD AGE the Old-Age Pension Act PENSION LOST ? against the granting of the pension to anyone who has received Poor-Law relief since January Ist this year met with some opposition in the House of Commons on the ground that it might inflict hardship upon deserving persons. An instance which seems to illustrate the point has already occurred at Hull. An old man of seventy-three years of age, otherwise qualified to receive the pension at the beginning of next year, applied to the Guardians for relief. He had been struggling

to keep his head above water, but age was against him and work was not to be found. So be was compelled at last to apply, and was granted the desired relief. Bat, as the law stands, he has lost his chance of obtainiag the pension to which he would otherwise have had good claim. In this case th 3 law apparently demanded that he should starve to death ia August that he might get five shillings a-week in the following Janu try. Tin condition, we are sorry to say, was too hard for him, and he succumbed to the pull of circumstances. There is obvious ground for a modification of the provisions in a case like this, in which the person is of deserving character and has no choice but to apply for relief or starve. The intention of the Government was never to penalise persons of that kind, and we are convinced that a regulation will be devised which will put an end to a harsh inter- pretation of the law in such a case.

An enterprising American WHY MEN Farr, journal declares dog. IN BUSINESS. matically that 93 per cent of the men who start in trade meet with failure. It approached a number of prominent business men—men presumably already among the elect, who did not succeed in failing, and who, therefore, know very little about the problem. Still, some of them deserve a little respect, and they have as much right as anyone else has to make guesses and utter words of Snailesian wisdom. One gentleman, who has evidently heard of Carlyle, believes we are all born fools, but some of us educate ourselves out of that way. He adds: "Most of the men who fail in business guess instead of know." That we have observed to be peculiarly an American weakness. Another sago remarks that the success- ful man considers the quality of an employee of greater importance than the salary to be paid. This is often undoubtedly true. " Success," says he, grandiloquently, "has its origin in the business man himself." " The main cause of failure," another platitudinist has discovered, "is lack of knowledge." The article which contains this delightful symposium ends impressively : " Men fail because they do things in the wrong way." We respectfully submit to our friends across the water that on another occasion they request opinion from a few men who have managed to fad. Their ideas would not be expressed in aphorism and epigram, but they might be of some profit.

Abdul Aziz may now be described as Abdul Azwaz ! * * _ _

The Borough Auditors Save presented their annual report this week. We assume that things are quite in order at the Town Hall, as the Auditors certify the accounts to be correct, and have no suggestions of importance to make.

* * * The youngest Parliamentary candidate at present in the field is Mr. John Lindeley, the Socialist candidate for the Barkston Ash Division of the West Riding. He is a native of Sunderland, twenty-ono years old, br twelve years has been in the accountants' depart- ment of the Newcastle Corporation, and is an effective speaker and writer. * * *

We are glad to see that the Health Committee are taking steps to ensure the sanitation and cleanliness of the public slaughter-houses. There is no more important work, short of providing a Municipal - abattoir. New regulations as to the constructions drainage, and ventilation of the slaughter-houses have been made and, we are glad to say, loyally accepted by the butchers.

* * * There should be no doubt about the cost of the new root-bridge at Howley coming well within the esti- mated £OOO, seeing that the Bridges Sub-Committee - recommends the acceptance of a tender at £485. ~ Whether the Council will agree to the letting of the , contract on Tuesday is, however, doubtful. On Thursday most of the members visited the proposed site, and there was anything but unanimity of feeling ; as to the spot where the bridge should be built. Howley people will be interested in the Council meeting on Tuesday. * 5 * When a Lancastrian visits London, much amuse- ment is had of his "provincial dialect." As a matter of fact, a student of Wiclif will tell you that all, or nearly all, of his peculiarities of speech are to be found in the writings of that great English scholar. The Lancashire dialect is, almost to a fault, simply Old English in pure and unmodernised form. Such a. defence cannot be raised on behalf of the Cockney's twang. Here are a few specimens found in certain London districts. " Binter tiker rome," he interprets, "Been to take her home" ; " Binuavinagime, ' as "Been having a game " ; "Hi in't ad no kike," as "I haven't had any cake," and "Biby's nime's Jimes" pline Jimes," as" Baby's name's James, plain James., It is far easier to recognise error than to discover truth.—Gocthe.

Our greatest glory is not in never failing, but in rising every time we fall.— Con f ucius. These be the ways of ladies, . . To those who love them, trials of our faith. T ennyson Life is a great and noble calling; not a mean and grovelling thing that we are to shuffle through as we can.—W. E . Gladstone.

There is a leaning to prosperity however obtained, and a prejudice in its favour.—Burke. It is well to believe that there needs but a little more courage, more love, more devotion to life, 3 little more eagerness one day to fling open wide the portals of joy and truth.—Maeterlinck. * * * If France has a problem to meet in the decline of its population there is an older difficulty of the same nature seeking solution at our own doors. Again the Y returns of the Registrar-General show a decline ie the population of Ireland. It is not that the deaths- exceed the births, but that the surplus is taken out of ; the country by emigration. Ireland is yearly contri- buting some of its best blood to America and to the Colonies. The entire population of Ireland is less than that of London. How to meet that situation has ' now been the almost hopeless task of statesmanship for many years. Conditions of life are improving ia the country, and the drain is not so great as it was, but it is more rapid than the natural increase in the "S population. HOIS to make Ireland more attractive to the younger Irish when new countries are holding out such openings to those who have been trained iii i agriculture may well dismay those responsible for 7] government in the absence of the development of I other industries over a great part of the country. * * * The Tradeston Liberal Unionist Association has

certainly taken a tolerant view of Mr. Cameron Corbett's new declaration of his political attitude. It has passed a resolution in these terms : That, having regard to Mr. Cameron Corbett's long connection with the constituency, his many valuable services, and the assurance given by him that his views on Home Rule are unchanged, the executive of the association see no cause to ask him to resign his seat at present. We note that the "Saturday Review," in dealing with the situation in anticipation, says : " A man who has convictions on only one question is not fit to represent Unionists anywhere." That is to be unnecessarily hard. Mr. Corbett has convictions on many questions, but apparently in only one direction do they agree with those of the " Saturday Review." That, how- ever, seems to be enough for the milder Unionism of the Tradeston Division. * * * Town-dwellers are apt in these bright and breezY summer days to forget that they have a smoke nuisance. A couple of months hence they will be much more conscious of the fact. Many towns are, of course, afflicted by the evil, and it is interesting to note what is being done in some of them to get rid of the trouble. In Hamburg, for instance, a scciety with , that object has been eminently successful. From a ' statement in " Chambers's Journal" we gather that not only does the society protect the general public but enables the manufacturer to secure a greater degree of efficiency from his fuel. The society tests various devices for overeomisg smoky chimneys, instructs stokers in the art of firing; suggests expedients for reducing smoke emission, fl periodically tests and overhauls the plant." Various fuels are tried by the society, with the idea of securiq those which have a high thermal value with the mill' mumlof smoke creation, and in certain cases stoke who reduce smoke emission from the furnaces un4g their control receive a bonus. All this seems eminentll useful work. We shall expect to hear shortly that Alderman Bennett is en route for Hamburg.

Sir Eyre Massey Shaw, whose death occurred on xuesday, was a great popular hero during his long and strenuous command of the Metropolitan Fire Brigade. Alert and soldierly in bearing, with a grey Pointed beard and a helmet of shining silver, Captain Paw was certainly a heroic figure at a great con- agration —a general of commanding presence, quick and sure judgment, and infinite resource. In his thirty years of London service he brought the fire gade to a state of unrivalled efficiency, e was the ideal "men on-the spot," many an instance being narrated of his extraordinary capacity for Teaching the scene of an outbreak, no matter what "?siness engaged him at the moment. So popular ,!Id he become that on the night "lolanthe " was pro- -In,ced at the Savoy, the house, cheered with delight en one of the chat acters, turning to a stall where tile redoubtable captain himself was seated, sang the w well-known lines:— Oh, Captain Shaw, Type of trae love kept under, Could thy brigade, With cold cascade Quench my great love, I wonder? The captain was an intimate friend of the King, who, as Prince of Wales, accompanied him more than once '34 a fire engine. Some ten years ago he lost a leg, Zad the other was amputated in December last, when e WaS seventy-eight years of age.
