div.head: POLITICS OF THE WEEK.
div.p: THE POLITICS OF THE WEEK.
[FROII OUR LONDON CORRESPONDENT.]

. • All the political questions which are most in men's Tiacis at the present moment group themselves :amid three centres, and from these centres radiate ellarnerable lines and cross-lines of inter-connection. r ia scarcely necessary to explain that these central Interests are tha peace of the civilized world, the progress of social reform, and the effect of tariffs upon national prosperity. But the progress of social reform le determined to a great extent by the exigencies of . revenue, and as these exigencies are largely created by the expenditure required for defence, it is by such an improvement in international relations as will relax the pressure of enormous armaments upon the revenue that sufficient resources are most likely to be •eSt free for social reform upon an ample scale. ,Again, tariffs affect international relations scarcely lees than they affect national prosperity. Free Trade, with its policy of the open door, removes ene of the most dangerous provocations to war. yet, as extremes tend to meet, even Protection, pushed to an extreme, may lead to the I,linainution of armaments by eventually depriving 'tticse nations which cling to it of the power to support 46. Ilul:rdPeenPetual strain. A protective tariff, 'imposing a upon the consumer far in excess of the benefit accruing to the revenue, makes it almost impossible for „a protectionist country to meet the demands of 'caoitions naval and military estimates out of current ev,cane. Such has been the experience of Germany, and,, our Consul-General at Frankfort, in his latest :?Part, alto points out that the increased cost of :letaal and fodder, owing to the duties upon their '23Portation, has caused one-third of the increased VPenditure of the German Army and Navy, and pro- increases of taxation in many directions. It is re tam of sound statesmanship to foster the prodac- ii," powers sad energy of a nation. These are s'llinpered and impoverished by the growth of exces- :re armaments and by a protectionist policy, but they are stimulated by wise social reforms.

Ora RELA.TIONS wall GERMANY. . Public attention has been closely directed to the 1 Wssibility of an agreement between this country and "mails' oi the basis of a limitation to the building °I warship ; and there has been much exercise of sPeculation, sometimes indiscreet and always, at any ', l'te, Premature. The German programme for the , "roan fleet, up to 1911, has been laid down in a law 6assea this year. It is not to be expected that the "roan Government would approach the Reichstag.to ~tseied this law, and to do so would certainly gure " ),18e to a mischievous agitation. But there are some 1 o:ootpeerfiuoln signs sa that Great Britain and Germany are period of more cordial relations. far,iendship between two nations which have been I °Oaring under mutual suspicions and misconceptions ,s a delicate plant, that may easily be injured by lioPatient handling. Patience, tact, and forbearance I,r,ti essential for the expansiorr of this budding amity. • riese qualities will not, we believe, be found wanting '°the statesmen and diplomatists who have charge of t ,fle affairs of the two nations. But it is not less impor- tant that they should be exhibited in the utterances of the organs of public opinion, of corporate bodies, '4,11C1 private individuals. When it has become fully 'o,tlized, both here and there, that there is no collision 2 Primary interests between the two countries in any loaner of the globe, and that "it is no part of our Palley,' as Sir Edward Grey said in the House of carlinons last July, "to give our friendships any hostile point towards any other Power . . . uor is it ,9iir object to isolate any Power whatever," a solid I°andation will have been laid for a future agreement, " i oh as a considerable majority of people n both !_ountries earnestly desires. There is great weight in Nit. Edward Grey's appeal to those who wish to form an opinion of the feeling of the two countries towards ach other "not to take short views." During the last twenty years there has been a time when there 1,, ,z as constant friction between this country and France; there has also been a time when there was constant Ir!ction between this country and Russia. Now that tfriction has been entirely removed. It would be absnrd I° Suppose that any friction which may have existed recent years between this country and Germany bill not give way before good intentions steadily carried out. BETTER USES FOR MONEY. If aroldgrudges and baseless distrust are not kept ire by busy-bodies and panic-mongers, we may :rPect the good sense of civilized peoples gradually (0 drive home the lesson that there are better uses for 111.11131 k money than to add battle-ship to battle-ship, t 2119 corps to army corps. When Germans are `-etiPjed with their "future on the water," they are Izet always thinking of the growth of naval arma- t,et,e• The other day Prince Ludwig of Bavaria, tfeal'ing at the banquet of the German Training Ship clic' en, expressed the desire of the Divarians to be 1 riectlY connected with the Weser and the Elbe, in (e'der that they may not be entirely cut off from the ,T-eat world traffic with the Baltic and the North Sea. ' the Germans naturally take a keen interest in their ba'vY, just as we tnke a great interest in our navy. tlut,,they would welcome the chance of diverting some t 4e Vast sums that they believe at present to be necessary for the navy, to the pacific and profitable Jet of developing inland navigation ; just as we "Plore the fact that while we devote sixty millions !Panally to naval and military expenditure, only the Vglith part of this gigantic sum could be set aside ,recently for Old Age pensions. And in the United etates we find people complaining that while millions are found , annually for armaments, not one adequate channel has been made from the great lakes to the poean for the billions of bushels of grain raised beyond Chicago. PrSHING ON WITH OLD AGE PENSIONS. The netspapers have been full of conjectures about e discussions that Mr. Lloyd-George is imagined to have held with German statesmen on the naval affairs °sl.Great Britain and Germany. Very little has been 1.,1,(1 about the main object of his visit to Germany. ' ic'e Chancellor of the Exchequer has been investigat. Ing the system of Imperial Old Age and Invalid surance,. mid acquainting himself with the ive t. Ler& attitude towards it. As he told a :e_Presentative of the Vienna IV eto F;;eie Presse the ~Fctliel to Old Age Pensions is an invalid fund and a ,iek fund. In the meantime there is to be no delay up the machinery of administration for Old i ° Pensions. The Local Government Board has • iPos_aed its regulations, accompanied by a Circular to the pe'al authorities. Meetings for the uppointment of thilasiau committees must be held before the end of all Month, or at such later date as the Board may blacP"'• At the end of next month forms of application th j be obtained, free of charge, at any post office, and it Postmaster is to give assistance in filling them up, tiill'ired• The pension officer who receives a claim Tbr report on it, and send it to the pensions committee. s„ eo days before their meeting the committee will tt":1. noiice to the claimants whose cases are to be i.)eusidered. After a claim has been approved, the cfllBioner will receive a book of pension orders, one whiel, i , each -- stone presented at the nearest post office fth is after the pension has begun to accrue a, i •th " 8, from January 1, 1000), when the amount of • weekly pension will be paid. TI, EIGHT HOURS FOR MINERS. -not he,Year's harvest of social legislation was of course Passiatf garnered in when Parliament adjourned after laa.l,e eg the Old Age Pensions Bill into law. Things asci,reltanged greatly since the time when Mr. Balfour the ed his followers that he would not " burden pa,T with overmuch legislation." The present ' letoent is not afraid of work. Licensing, Educa. i _

tion, Housing and Town-planning, the Port of London, the Protection of Children, and an Eight Hours Day for Miners are among the problems with which Parliament will grapple when it meets for the autuma sitting. It is remarkablehaw the attitude of Con- servatives has changed towards this last question since they went into Opposition. Formerly they were agreed that, when the miners could settle their differences in regard to the eight boars day, there was no reason why it should not be adopted. Now tha those differences have been settled, the Conservatives have developed a sudden hostility to the measure which embodies what was Once with them a pious aspiration. Any sincere apprehension that may have been felt in any quarter regarding the effect of such a measure is concerned with the possibility of a rise in price through a reduction in output. Mr Russell Rea, who was the chairman of the committee that inquired into the probable economic effects of the Bill, has stated that he should not be surprised if there was no increase at all in the price of coal, and that, at any 'rate, only during the period of transitiod Could there be any disturbance of equilibrium. Provision has been made in the Bill for the contingency of a temporary dislocation. But as the coal-owners have said that they prefer a change all at once to a gradual one, it may be doubted whether their professed appre- hensions are very strongly felt. The Labour members contend that not less work will be done in the shorter time, but possibly more. It is the time during which the miner Is actually working, not the length of his stay underground, that determines the output, , and it is impossible that work in cramped positions and in circumstances injurious to health I can be carried on for nine or ten hours II continuously. Both the importance of the industry to the nation and its dangerous character point to the necessity of Government regulation on behalf of the security of those who work in the mines. Of the dangerous trades which are recognised as calling for Government supervision, the miners' work is not the least dangerous. The Eight Hours Bill can rightly be oonsidered as part of a consistent policy to "make life brighter, easier, richer, more fruitful for the bulk of our fellow-countrymen," and "proper and regular hours of healthy labour are the only foundation on which a highly complicated system of Industry can stand.," But the measure has an especial urgency over other parts of this policy because it aims at increasing the security of human life. The longer the hours, S 3 the Home Secretary, as well as several of the miners' representatives, reminded the House of Commons in the second read- ing debate, the greater is the risk of accident. HOW PROTECTION IS WORKING TO-DAY. _ _

-- • - - - - - -- An illuminating view of the working of a highly organized system of Protection is afforded by the report of our Consul-General at Frankfort, to which reference has already been made above. The German agrarian duties have so enhanced the cost of all necessary food-stuffs, that the Chamber of Commerce of Bremen speaks of a general dearth of victuals. The working man found himself unable to live upon his wages, and the manufacturer consequently now fipds himself under the necessity of paying higher wages. From this proceeds a further consequence, that the cost of manufacture is increased and the export trade declines. Yet the working man has no benefit from the higher wage. It is swallowed up by the greater cost of living. Nor is the home market strengthened, as in normal conditions, by the increased aggregate of wages. The workman has no margin of extra purchasing power. It is all he can do to buy sufficient food for himself and his family. On the ' manufacturer of highly finished articles Protection presses with multiplied force. For the raw material, the half-finished product, and the machinery required for his business, he has to pay a price enhanced by heavy t iriffs, if it comes from abroad, or still more enhanced if he buys it at home, by the operations of the syndicate that is able to regulate its rates at will, because it is protected by an insuperable tariff wall. The situation into which industrial Germany has been brought by a "scientific tariff" can be summarized briefly thus :—The manufacturer has to pay an increased price for labour because the landlord pockets, in rent, the excess in the price of food-stuffs over the natural price; and he has to pay an extravagant price for his raw material and for his machinery. The working man has less work, because the export trade suffers by this artificial dearness ; he suffers from the" dearth of victuals," and though he obtains a nominally higher wage, fails to obtain one which recoups him for what he loses -through the greater cost of his food.

Alleged Embezzlement at Warrington. At the Borough Court on Thursdan before Mr. John Fairclongh and other magistrates,i'Villiam Wicking- ton, of Canterbury-street, was charged with having embezzled sums of 18s. 6d. and 10s. received by him on account of his master, William Powell, florist, of Padgate and Warrington market. —The Chief Constable in applying for seven days' remand, said prisoner surrendered himself on Wednesday evening to Police- Sergeant Hesp. Prisoner worked at the stalls in the Market-place, and it was alleged that he received sums of money and failed to account for them. The remand was granted bail being allowed, himself in £lO and one surety of £5. The Memorial to Miss Willis. At the last Quarterly meeting of the Church C,uncil, held on Monday, July 6th (says "The Warrington Parish Church Parochial Magazine") it was agreed to invite six tenders, three trona Warrington firms and three from well-known wood carvers outside the town, for the erection of Mr. Segar Owen's beautiful design. At a special meeting of the Council called last month for the purpose, these tenders were laid before the members, and that of Messrs. Garnett, of Warrington, the lowest, for £035 was accepted. We are sure that in Messrs. Garnett's hands the work will be well done. , The amount received and promised up to the present is, we understand, £3Ol.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, August 29, l9OB.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, August 29, l9OB.

Another Prize for Crosfleld's Band. I At Workington, on Saturday, the 100 guineas silver cup, presented by Sir John Randles, M.P., was NVOII outright by Goodshaur after a re-play. Crosfield's were awarded the second prize.

Sale of Pigs at Walton Hall. A sale of fifty-nine pedigree large and middle white Yorkshire pigs from the famous herd owned by Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., was held at Walton Hall, on Thursday, by Mr. Bainbridge. The total proceeds amounted to about 210 guineas, the largest amount for one animal being ten guineas. The principal purchaser was Mr. Stephenson, West Derby-road, Liverpool,who bought nine animals.

, Unpunetnality Expensive. I A youth named John Broughton was charged a the Borough Police Court on Monday with using at lurry on the Wilderspool-causeway at 10 p.m. on the 15th August without having a lighted lamp, attached to it. Defendant did not appear when the case was , called on a few minutes after ten o'clock and the case was heard in his absence.—P.C. Gibson proved the case.—The Mayor said that probably a lighter sentence I would have been imposed if the defendant had appeared, but as he had not done so he I would be fined 10s. and costs-20s. in all.— Close upon eleven o'clock the defendant put in an lappearance, and the Clerk asked him why he was not I present when the Court opened at ten o'clock.—To this defendant who appeared to be quite enconcerned) replied: cou(ld not get. I had other things to look after. (LaUghter.)—The Clerk : But you ought to have been here at ten.—Defendant said it was not con- venient to be present.—The Mayor: You are an hour , late. If you had come to us in a civil manner and explained, why, we might, have re-considered our decision. But it seems that you do' not care. We , should have opened he case but for your impertinence. I We shall let the fine:stand.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

HILL CLIFFS AND STOCKTON HEATH UNITED BAND OF HOPE.—The annual meeting of this Society to elect officers and arrange the work of the coming Session was held in the Wesleyan schoolroom on Eriday evening. This Society, formed several years ago by the three Free Churches of the district, has carried on a good work among the rising generation in promoting the interests of total abstinence. A large and representa- tive Committee has been appointed from the various schools and a good number put in an appearance at the meeting which angers well for the future work of the coming winter. The Rev. J. S. Hughes presided. The retiring officers were thanked for their services and the following were appointed for the coming session:— President, Mr. Arthur Mounfield ; vice-presidents, Rev. J. S. Hughes, Mr. H. Brereton, Mr. J. Moss, Mr. Deakin and Mr. Pearse ; treasurer, -Miss Mounfield ; secretary, Mr. G. Whitfield ; assistant secretary, Miss Ellison ; registrar, Miss Hall; superintendents, Messrs. A. Jones, J. Pearce and J. Moss ; organist, Mr. G. Arthur Whitfield ; assistant organist, Master T. Pearse. Representatives to Council of Warrington Band of Hope Union, Messrs. (1 Whitfield, J. Whitfield and A. Jones. It was decided to join in the great forward movement of the Lancashire and Cheshire Band of Hope Union to be held in Manchester during October. The arrangements for commencing the winter work in September were completed, the committee being most enthusiastic for the work of the Society.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
"A Woman Worth Winning."

This drama, presented for the first time in Warring- ton by Mr. Percy Norman's company, is a stirring story of Russian life in which tyranny and suffering, pathos and humour all play a part. The author (Mr. A. B. Mackay), has made skilful use of the material at his disposal, and the result is a play which works up excitement to fever heat. The villain has pursued his work so relentlessly as to arouse a storm of indig- dation in the gallery, while the hero and heroine have been enthusiastically acclaimed. There are many thrilling situations, notably the explosion which checks the pursuit of the escaped convicts who have taken refuge in the forest, and the duel between Roma Pauloff, disguised as a soldier, and General Borinski, her persecutor. Ur. A. B. Mackay, the author, as General Borinski, is one of thee leading spirits of the play. He poartrays the cruel and-unscrupulous officer in a thorough-going fashion and with complete success. Miss Chrism Dunbar soon establishes herself a favourite by her fine, dramatic acting as Roma Pauloff and carries off a large share of the honours. Mr. Carthage Caldcleugb, as Ivan Bardoff, presents a remarkable character study, weird and fascinating, and shows himself to be possessed of talents of a high order. Mr. George Edwin Clive is a dashing and impulsive Fergus Lovinsky. The many humorous interludes prove highly popular, and in these Mr. , Louis Newman as Bertie Scribbles, Mr. Ernest Kendrick as Peter Poppies, and Miss Ida Mackay as 1 Katerina Moss, all do well and provoke much glee. The mounting of the play is elaborate and in the best of taste.

div.head: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME. "CHARLEY'S AUST."
div.p: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME. "CHARLEY'S AUST."

Local playgoers will be pleased to hear that next week the ever popular " Charley's Aunt " will be pre- sented by Mr. Brandon Thomas' (the author's) own company, transferred here after the recent successful season at the Royalty Theatre, London. The reputa- tion of this excellent comedy and of the company should be sufficient to attract crowded houses, and visitors to the theatre next week are assured of a delightful evening's merriment. " Charley's Aunt " will be preceded by" The Lancashire Sailor," also written by Mr. Brandon Thom is.

div.head: MORE BETTING CASES.
div.p: MORE BETTING CASES.
Heavy Fines Imposed.
POLICE OFFICER ASSAULTED.

The crusade against street betting in Warrington is being vigorously continued, and two more cases were heard by the Borough Bench yesterday.—James Whaley, labourer, 77, Cartwright-street, was charged with loitering in a publio passage at the rear of Cart • wright-street on Thursday afternoon for the purpose of betting. He pleaded guilty. The Chief Constable said Sergeant Stuart and Constable Clough were on duty in the vicinity of the passage at 12.45. They kept defendant under observa- tion and saw him take betting slips from five men and two women. They also saw him pay over to others money which was apparently the outcome of the pre- vious day's transactions. He was arrested and taken to the police station, and in his possession were found £1 15s. 4d. in cash, a handicap book, and a slip contain- ing the names of ten horses. Defendant made a state- ment to the effect that the betting slips he had taken had been handed over to his employer, from whom he received a weekly wage of 20s. The blayor said the Bench were determined to put down betting. Defendant would be fined £lO and costs with the option of a month's imprisonment and there was no doubt that in any other cases of that kind which were clearly proved the fine would not be less than £lO in future.

Joseph Lawrenson, 40, Forster-street, pleaded guilty to a similar offence at the rear of Forster-street and also to having been previously convicted. The Chief Constable said that about 1.20 on Thursday 'afternoon, P.C. Woollacott saw the prisoner take betting slips from two men. He kept him under observation for ten minutes and then went to arrest him. Prisoner dashed into his house but was eventually arrested on a warrant. Wnilst in the house, the officer , saw the prisoner take from his pocket money and slips' and hand them to his friends, the constable being pre- I vented from taking possession of them. Prisoner was fined £lO and costs for a similar offence on Augiist 4th. The magistrates imposed a fine of £2O and costs or three months, with the warning that if prisoner came I before them again he would probably be sent to gaol without the option of a fine. James Lawrenson, jun., 40, Forster-street, and Thomas William Lawrenson, 3.3, Warburton-street, were then charged with having assaulted P.C. Woollacott in Forster-street. The Chief Constable said tho case arose out of the last one. Woollacott followed Joseph Lawrenson into the house and was set upon by James Lawrenson who knocked him about while Thomas William held -his arms. This continued for some little time in the house, Woollacott being struck several times in the face and kicked on the legs and lower portion of the body. He eventually got into the street where the assaults were continued. The Chief Constable asked the Bench to inflict such a penalty as would act as a deterrent.

• P.C.Voollacett gave evidence b-e.aring out this state- ment. He said botj the prisoners knew him and when they were assaulting him they exclaimed " Mr.— Woollacott, again I" The prisoner James Lawrenson said they did not I know the officer as he was wearing faoleskins and had 'his face blacked.

It was stated that James Lawreruicon bad been before the Court five times previously. Both prisoners were fined £5 and costs or two months imprisonment, the Mayor remarking that the Bench were determined to put a stop to such conduct.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.

ST. HELEN'S MAN INJURED ON THE RAILWAY Early on Sun dalmorning a man named PatriekDonery, a young man, residing at 104, Rowen-street, St. Helens, was found on the railway line at Edge-lane Station. He was conveyed on the horse ambulance to the Royal Infirmary, where it was found that be was suffering from severe injuries to the head. When in a semi- conscious state he was understood to say that he had fallen out of a train. He was reported to have had money about him, but no railway ticket.

div.head: VETERAN POSTAIAN'S DEATH.
div.p: VETERAN POSTAIAN'S DEATH.

On Monday the remains were interred at the St. Helens Cemetery of Mr. T. Bonney, of Talbot-street, who was one of the oldest postmen in the United Kingdom. Owing to slackness in the watch trade, to which he had served his time, he became a postman in 1859, but in 1874 resumed his business as a watchmaker. Shortly afterwards he became armourer-sergeant to the old 47th South Lancashire Regiment, and abont eight or nine years ago he retired from that position with a pension. He died on Friday afternoon last, and leaves grown-up DRUNKEN FOOTBALLER FINED.

On Monday *at St. Helens Police Court, David Traynor) who was formerly one of the most prominent Northern Union three-quarters in Lancashire, was brought up on a charge of being drank and disorderly, to which hepleaded.guilty. A constable stated that on Saturday night prisoner was drunk in the market, creating a disturbance, and threatening one of the stall- holders. Asked what he had to say, Traynor said he was very drunk. The prisoner, who had been before the , Court fifteen times previously, was fined ss. and costa ' with the alteinative of seven days' hard labour.
ORANGE DEMONSTRATION AT ST. HELENS:

The annual demonstration of the St. Helens and district lodges of the Loyal Orange institution was held at Parr on Sunday afternoon . For many years past service has been held in St. Peter's Church, Parr, where the service was conducted by the" Rev. W. Edmondson, who resigned somo time ago, and who was known as an enthusiastic supporter of the Order. On this occasion the service was held in a field off Chancery-lane. The members, to the number -of over 300, assembled at Nunn-street, and marched In procegion through the village to the field. At the head of tbe procession there as carried the large banner of the Order, and underneath it there walked four little girls, carrying the open' Bible. The procession was accompanied by the Victoria Band, the Colonel Saunderson Band, and the Protestant Boys' Band, all of Liverpool ; and among those present were many Liverpool members of the Order, including Bro. T. Brady, P.G.M. J. Holden, P.G.T.Btewart ill`Coy, and Bro. J. Adams, Bro. Lister, and Bro. Kearns (Bootle.) The service was conducted by Bro. T. Brady,, who delivered an address, taking as his test the words, lhy faith, bath made thee whole." Special hymns wets sung, and the procedings terminated with the singing of the National Anthem,

div.head: LABOUR MEETING AT ST. HELENS. MR. T. GLOVER, M.P., AND THE ABRAI DISASTER.
div.p: LABOUR MEETING AT ST. HELENS. MR. T. GLOVER, M.P., AND THE ABRAI DISASTER.

On Monda night Mr. T. Glover, M.P., addressed a Labour meeting at St. Helena, which was presided over by Councillor P. Phythian, and, referring to the Com- pensation Act, said its provisions were sufficient proof that the Labour men of this country had done some- thing in the House of Commons to better the condition of the workers of the .country. (Applause). There had been a measure before the House of Commons for no less than twenty-one years with reference to an eight hours day for miners and he himself had been lobbying for twenty years to try to obtain an eight hours day for miners. It had passed the second reading six times, and six times it had been defeated. Now, when it had passed the second reading without any opposition in the House of Commons, they saw the Coal Consumer's League trying to prevent it becoming law. ("Shame.") They maintained it would increase the price of coal ; but the statistics showed that the average working hours of the collier at present were seven and a quarter hours a day, and if they had an eight hours day it would mean, instead of an increased price and a lesser production, an increased production of 20,000,000 or 30,000,000 tons a year. (Applause.) On the other hand, the miners considered eight I hours too long, but they were prepared to accept an eight hours day. (Hear, hear.) Those people who talked in that strain should remember how seventy-five men were plunged into eternity in a minute of time through the colliery explosion at Abram. He asserted that if the first rule in the Coal Mines Regula- tion Act had been carried out there could not have been that explosion. The first rule in the Mines Act was that an adequate supply of air should be maintained in all the working places to render the gas harmless, and if that had been done the explosion could never have taken place. He hoped they would be able to find out what had been the cause of this lamentable explosion, whereby seventy-five men had been plunged into eternity. It would cost the employers something like £lO,OOO to £15,000 in compensation, which would be some morsel of comfort to those left behind. (Applause.

div.head: NEWTON HORTICULTURAL SHOW.
div.p: NEWTON HORTICULTURAL SHOW.

The 23rd annual show, of the Newton-le-Willows Horticultural Society took place on Saturday. Fine weather prevailed and the proceedings were very successful. There were over 800 entries, a higher num- ber than ever before, and the produce was voted to be of all-round excellence; the vegetables in both amateurs and oottagers, classes comparing with the best in England. Special prizes were offered for the best window plant grown, by scholars attending day schools ii area 30 of the County Education Committee, and the special for the best in these classes was won by Olive Spottiswoode (Earlestown Wesleyans). A pro- gramme of sports was gone through, the prizes being presented to the winners by Mrs. A. C. Leslie. The chief prize winners were—Open : W. Collingwood, L. E. Whittaker, J. Smith, C. R. Pilkington, J. Randall, T. Clore and A. Smith. Amateurs: A. Cotterill, R. Brown, H. Newport, W. T. Strange, Warren and Davies, Mrs. Bent, T. Lowe, W. Parnell and T. Fazakerley. Cottagers O. Day, S. Davenport, Mrs. O'Neill, A. Sandeman. Cottage gardens: W. Septon' .1. Hassell, W. Parnell, J. Hewitt and W. Beaman. The Earlestown Prize Band played a selection of musio during thea after Soon and for dancing in the evening. After the judges had finished their labours, they sat down to well served luncheon at the White Lion Inn.

div.head: DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MR. HENRY HOUGHTON.
div.p: DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MR. HENRY HOUGHTON.

The death occurred on Thursday night list week of Mr. Henry Houghton, the oldest public official in this district. He has been lying ill with heart trouble for some weeks at his house. Park-rcad, Newton,and had suffered from the complaint for a long time, though attending to his duties till recently. He TM rate collector for the Urban District Council, and for the , Newton Improvement Commissioners since 1868. He , had also been poor rate collector and assistant overseer for the Warrington Union for many years. His age was 73. Mr. Houghton was an old Freemason, and a Volunteer from the beginning of that movement in 1859, being in fact, the oldest corporal in the country. The funeral took place at St. Peter's Churchyard on Monday', the Rev. J. Ryder officiating assisted by the Rev. Walcott. The coffin was carried the church by a number of members of the Volunteer Corps. The coffin was wrapped in a Union Jack. The mourners were the three sons of the de:eased, Messrs. Henry George. and Frank Houghton, Mr. George Houghton (brother of deceased), and his nephews, Messrs. Eddie and George (Liverpool), and W. and A. Egerton Mr. A. W. Anderton Ison-in-law) and Mr. H. Egerton, Next came members of the Council, namely, Messrs. T. Ormond (chairman), C. B. F. Borron, A. Smith, M. Seton, W. Collingwood, and J. Higham, followed by the Council officials- and clerks, including Messrs. C. Cole (clerk to the Council), R. Surtees (clerk of the works), J, Bowes (surveyor). T. Swift, C. D. Mayor, Gee, Clewth, Foley, Dickinso (assistant overseer, Haydock). Tunstall (late Grand Master of Oddfellows), Owen, Hesvvall, Cheshire ; Horridge, Heaton, T. Ireland, T. Hewitt, G. Moon and P, Fairclough. This annual summer show was held on Thursday afternoon at /lalton-view, and was opened by Mrs. Fred Neil, in the presence of a largo gathering. The exhibits show an increase upon last year, and the quality all round was excellent. There was an abundant supply of fruit, vegetables, flowers, bread, Sic. div.head: INSPECTOR UNDER ALKALI ACT.
div.p: INSPECTOR UNDER ALKALI ACT.

The joint committee representing Liverpool and the Widnes district appointed to nominate for appointment by the Local Government Board an inspector under the Alkali Act met at the Liverpool municipal buildings on Monday, and selected Mr. Potter (a well-known inspector already under the Board) for the office. There were about forty candidates. The duties comprise an outside supervision of works liable to emit noxious fumes, and a co-operation with the management in the prevention of public nuisance. The commencing salary is £5OO per annum.

div.head: ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.
div.p: ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.

On Monday morning a man named Peter Joyce, of 13, Bold-street, Altrincham, was admitted to the Widnes Accident hospital as an in-patient, suffering from a broken leg. Joyce was found about 4.20 on Monday morning under a railway arch, near \Vest Bank Docks with his left leg broken, by P.S. Smith and P.C. Robinson. It appears that he fell on some railway metals on West Bank Dock while going down to the water intending to work his passage down to Liverpool.

div.head: RURCORN LIBRARY COMIITTEE.
div.p: RURCORN LIBRARY COMIITTEE.

IThe annual meeting of the Runcorn Free Library Committee was held at the Town Hall last Friday evening. There were present Messrs. W. Handley ; (chairman), F. W. Hutton, S. Pope, T. Riley and F. C. Druce, and Mrs. Jones (librarian).—Authority was given ,to the librarian to have 100 volumes re-bound.---The : Librarian read the 26th annual report which stated / that in the lending and reference eepartments more volumes have been issued than in any previous year. , The number of borrowers' tickets issued during the year was 1,069, being a decrease of 29 compared with , last year. Five hundred and eighty-seven tickets were , issued to males and 482 to females. Twenty-four tickets have been issued to subscribing members being non-residents. The lending department has been open / 153 afternoons and 251 evenings. The afternoon issues amounted to 5,137 and the evening issues to 32,55. The total number of book issued from the lending library was 37,719, being an increase of 4,811 compared with last year. The number of books issued from the reference department was 1,789, an increase of six compared with last year. The total number of books issued during the year was 39,503, an increase compared with last year of 4,850. The average , daily issue was 155, an increase of two compared with last year. The highest daily average was 189 and the lowest 132. During the year 290 volumes had been added to the library stock, 217 volumes in the lending library, 236 of which were purchased and 11 presented. :In the reference library 43 volumes were added, 19 of which were purchased and 24 presented. Two hundred and fifty volumes had been re-bound, 83 worn-out books had been replaced and six lost books had been paid for and , replaced. Every book was accounted for at the annual , stock-taking. The total number of volumes in the library at the end of the year was 11,090. The Com- mittee express thanks to the various donors of money, books, periodicals and newspapers. The Chairman, in moving the adoption of the report and an instruction for 150 copies to be printed, said it was a very satisfactory record of work and reflected the greatest possible credit upon the librarian as a clear and succinct statement. Upon his suggestion the committee approved the addition to the report of a paragraph recording that arrangements were made during the year for a course of Gilchrist lectures. HIGHER SPitNDARD SCHOOL FOR RUNCORN.
LORD STANLEY OF ALDERLEY ON EDUCATIONAL PROGRESS.

lOn Wednesdsy afternoon, before a large assembly, Lord Stanley of Alderley opened a new , higher standard school and manual instruction centre at Runcorn. The school is built ou elevated hind at Balfour-road, from the designs of Mr. James Wilding, the town surveyor, and the contractors were Messrs. Dolan and Son, of Warrington. The cost of the building and site is about £12,000. The main block stands in the centre of the playgrounds, and accommo- dates 300 boys on the ground-floor and 300 girls on the I first floor. The architect presented Lord Stanley with I a silver key of chaste design. The large company assembled in the central hall, under the presidency of Mr. James Pritchard, chairman of Runcorn Education Committee. I Lord Stanley, in the course of his address, referred , to the immense progress made in education during the 'last thirty years. That building, excellent as it was, only showed the increasing standard of efficiency that , was demanded by the public authorities in the provision of education for the children of the nation. They in the North of England—Lancashire and Cheshire—had in some ways suffered in these later days through the ' activity of their forefathers. In the early part of the nineteenth century, certainly before the passing of the I Education Act, they were more active in self-help and in organising for the social needs of the people in I these great manufacturing districts than the rest I of the country ; and it had happened to the people of Lancashire and Cheshire what sometimes happened to people who were at one time foremost in the race, they were content with what they had done, and did not generally recognise what they had to do. The Cheshire County Council recognised the necessity of having not only good schools, but properly-trained teachers, and I were establishing a training college at Crewe. I (Applause.) Lately there had been some lugubrious I letters to the papers complaining that there was an I over supply of training accommodation, and that many students in training colleges were apprehensive that when they came out they would not find employment. , That apprehension was to a certain extent founded 'no fact, but he believed there would be no real difficulty in finding places for students now in college, and students who would go into training in a few years. If they were to have the same proportion of certificated and trained teachers in English schools as there were in Scotch schools, they would have some 27,000 to 30,000 more trained and certificated teachers employed than they now had. Lord Stanley strongly advocated that no teacher should have a class of more than thirty or forty scholars. He spoke in high terms of apprecia- tion of the new school and the work it was intended to do. Dr. Hodgson, chairman of the County Education Committee, said the school was an experiment which would ho vv•atchel with interest throughout Cheshire. They were going to give boys and girls a better chance when they reached the most adaptive stage of the fourth standard. A vote of thanks was passed to the speakers on the motion of Archdeacon Wood. seconded by Mr. NV. Handley. After vards the visitors were entertained to afternoon tea.

div.p: Accident to Mr. H. P. Mortimer,

Oa Saturdly afternoon a serious accident happoaed to Mr. 11. P. Mortimer, of Crofton Lodge, Kingsley, who, accompanied by a friend, was returning from Frodsham. The horse they were driving bolted, and with great speed ran down Guessy's Slack•road, which is most dangerous. div.head: COLLIERY DISASTER.
div.p: THE COLLIERY DISASTER.
SHILLING FUND OPENED AT WARRINGTON.

The public sympathy aroused by the terrible colliery disaster which has Plunged the village of Abram, near Wigan, into mourning, and deprived many a , family of the breadwinner, is finding tangible expres- sion in the generous support given to the various funds opened for the relief of the dependents of the victims and of those who have been so suddenly thrown out of work by last week's tragedy. Warring- ton must not be behind in this truly charitable work of relieving immediate want and we are glad to be able to announce that the Mayor has opened a shilling fund which, we believe; will be liberally supported.

div.head: MAYOR'S LETITP. AND OFFER.
div.p: THE MAYOR'S LETITP. AND OFFER.

On hearing of the disaster, his Worship at once wrote to the Mayor of Wigan as under : Let me assure you on behalf of the inhabitants of Warrington and myself of our deepest sympathy with Your fellow townsmen aad yourself in the great calamity which has occurred in your midst. We grieve especially for the sad loss of life, and our sincere hope is that the Great Comforter of all may shower the blessings of true peace and resigna- ion to His will upan all who are now any ways afllicted and distressed.

We are, at the same time, proud to think that the ancient town of Wigan can in such times of trouble boast of men who rank with the "bravest of the brave" in trying to save their comrades. Again assuring you lof any help that lies in my po Nen , WIGAN'S THANKS AND ACCEPTANCE. ' The Mayor of Wigan replied : The Mayor's Parlour, Wigan, August 21, 1908. My dear Mayor Smethurst,—Permit me to thank you and your people for you: sympathetic letter. The prompt response to our appeal is a bright spot in the dark cloud caused by the Maypole disaster, and we shall value any help you can give us in raising funds for the benefit of the widows and orphans of the 75 men who perished and the families of the 809 men now thrown out of employment. As lam advised that at least three months will elapse before the pits can be re-opened we shall need every penny that can be raised.
Again thanking you for your letter, I am, yours faithfully, Stu WOOD.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

There is a very bright programme at the Palace and Hippodrome this week, and the seeker after entertainment is well repaid with a visit to the place. Quite a unique turn is provided by Larola, who performs numerous feats of strength and dexterity in a way which compels laughter as well as admiration. We have not seen quicker" business "than Larola's for some time, and there is not a dull second while he is on the stage. The Glenroy troupe of vocalists and international dancers charm both the eye and the ear with their singing and costume dancing. One does not often find an infirmity turned to good account, but Messrs. Con- way and Leland, the Merry Mouopedes, show us how to rise superior to misfortune. These two artistes have only one log each, but they combine together for the entertainment of the public in a most remarkable manner. Some of their feats of agility are surprising, while the absence of a leg here and there only seems to add to the opportunities for trickery. They are two merry fellows and get along much better than tho majority of folks who are blessed with the usual "understandings." Rose Cabini_ancl Noralt Noble are attractive comediennes, and both oblige with a pleasing song and dance. W. G. Wesley is . a character comedian of parts, and his song " Too far " proves a very pipular number. Deans and Wilton are eccentric comedy acrobats., There are plenty of the kind on the boards, but few have such an eye for humorous effect as the pair under notice. James Howard and Fanny St. Clair appear in the comedy sketch " Do you want to buy any coke ?" which we may say at once is not worth the trouble bestowed upon it by the artistes. They might easily produce a more original and entertaining turn. Raymond's bin-tableaux are again excellent while Mr. Widdep's orchestra leaves little to be desired in the way of musical accompani- ment.

NEXT WEEK'S PROC;PAIIIIE. An attractive programme is promised for nest week, the bill being headed by the wonderful and artistic Solbins, sensational trick cyclists. The other artistes will be : —Annie Schuberth in the original song scena "The Deputy" ; Violet Nunn, singer of coon songs; Edwards and Dacre, in comedy duologue entitled " What a life " ; George James, comedian ; Tossing Austins, American comedy jugglers and dancers ; T. Thornbury, artist in sand, smoke and oil ; harry Luck, comedian.

TOWN COUNCIL. Business of the Next Meeting. The monthly meeting of the Town Council will be held on Tuesd,ty evening when the following, among other business, will be considered :

AUDITORS' REPORT. The following report of the Borough Auditors has been presented to the Finance and Estates Committee. Warrington, 25th July, 1903. To THE 3.1.AY0R, ALDER:n.IEN AND BURGESSES OF THU CORPORATION OF WARRINGTON. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, We have examined the Borough Treasurer's Accounts of the various departments of the Corporation for the year ending 31st March, 1933 (exclusive of the Educa- tion a?partment), together with the invoices and vouchers relating thereto and certify that we find them correct. The various stock accounts are certified by the responsible official in each case. • We have also inspected several books of account not usually kept at the Borough Treasurer's Office, among others those at the Tramways Office, Markets, Museum and Bowling Green, and find them in good order. The principal officials of the Treasurer's Department are covered by a guarantee policy which has been pro- duced to us, but we wish to point out that the heads of several other departments handling considerable and increasing sums of money are not so covered. The deeds in charge of the Town Clerk have been exhibited to us. Yours faithfully, W. J. WILSON, Mayor's Auditor. LAURENCE BoLcos, 1 Elective E. ENGLAND, f Auditors. REGULATION OF SLAUGHTER-HONES. The following deputation of the Butchers' ASSOCIA.- tion waited upon the Health Committee on August 20th :—Messrs. Bowcock, W. Shaw. R. C. Shaw, R. I'. Bridge, E. Wright, and the manager of Messrs. %V and R. Fletcher. The deputation was introduced by Mr. Councillor Singleton. The recommendations with regard to slaughter-houses were laid before them, After discussion the deputation, having agreed in principle to the whole of the requirements, were informed that each individual owner or tenant of a slaughter-house would receive a copy of the Committee's requirements with regard to their slaughterhouse, and that a Sub- Committee of the Health Committee would be appointed for the purpose of meeting the owner or tenant and hearing his views thereon.

MEDICAL INSPECTION OF SCHOOL CHILDREN. At a meeting of the Heath Coromittee on August 25th the Town Clerk reported that in accordance with the instructions of the Committee,he had,in conjunction with the Medical Officer of Health and the Director of Education, agreed upon the following with respect to the medical inspection of school children That the duties of the Medical o.ficer of Health in relation to the Education Committee be those set forth in the conditions of his appointment and that he be the responsible officer in respect of the medical inspection ; That the detailed medical inspection be carried oat by the Assistant Medical Officer of Health, who will be mainly concerned with the individual inspection of school children. When not occupied in this work his ser ;ices shall be at the disposal of the Medical Officer of Health for public health work (other than the general infectious disease work) of the town. The following are the proposals for carrying out the details, viz. : (1) The Medical Inspection Committee will instruct the Director of Education to furnish the names of the children admitted to and leaving school and to make arrangements (i.e., directions to teachers, etc.) for the individual's examination at each school ; As a register and cards hare to be filled in in respect of each child, it will be necessary to provide some clerical assistance for the School Medical Officer ; such clerical assistance, together with weighing machines and other apparatus, to be provided by the Medical Inspection Committee • The register 93 compiled will be sent to the Medical Inspection Committee with the reports of the School Medical Officer ; The Medical Inspection Committee will be respon- sible for dealing with the cases after examination by the School Medical Officer, and that Committee will make their own arrangements as to remedial measures. Resolved that the same be approved. THE SELECTION OF MAYOR. The General Purposes Committee has resolved that the meeting for the selection of Mayor be held on the 25th September next.

THE NEW FOOT-ERIDGE AT HOWLEY. The following resolution of the Bridges Sub-Com- mittee was read Resolved, that the Council be recommended to accept the tender of Messrs. D. Powell and Co. of Westminster, for the erection of a Suspension Bridge at Howley at a cost of £485." The Council inspected the proposed site on Thursday, but no decision was come to. WIDENING OF BETTERMARKF.T-STREET. The Town Clerk reported to the General Purposes Committee that in accordance with the instructions of the Council at their last meeting he proposed to apply for a Provisional Order for the acquisition of the properties required for the widening of Buttermarket- street, andsequested the instructions of the Committee as to the inclusion of other properties in the draft order. The matter was referred to the Street Improvement Committee.

THE BEAMONT SCHOOL Children's Garden Day. A " g[trdeu day" in connection with an elementary school is an occasion hitherto unheard of in War- rington. It has remained for the Beamont Council School to introduce this pleasing innovation. Yester- day was the first " Garden Day " and parents of tke scholars and members of the Education Cummitteo were invited to visit the school and see what has been done by the children in the way of gardening. The Beamont School with its spacious playgrounds is admirably adapted for initiating the young folk into the delights of horticulture and it goes without saying that the scholars have entered into this part of their education with zest. ' There are gardens at the front of the school for which the children as a body make themselves responsible, but in the tending of the gardens in the playgrounds separate plots are alotted to individuals. The scheme has worked most successfully, the youthful gardeners having taken the greatest pride in their work, and a week or two ago the gardens were a blaze of colour. oi-en now they are looking very, pretty and the parents were delighted to have the opportunity of inspecting them under the guidance of the scholars who were specially told off to explain anything they wished to know. What was even more pleasing was that the school itself was thrown open and visitors were able to witness lessons, in progress. They were invited to " walk about quite freely, only refraining from speaking to yocir It was a revelation to many to see how educational me..hods have changed of late years. At Beamont school the system is splendidly up-to-date and has been planned to be of utility in the commerce of the town. Some of the elder scholars were receiv- ing instruction in science, whilst other interesting subjects were cardboard modelljug, paper folding, brush drawing, and clay modelling. The members of the "babies' class " were to be seen comfortably seated in armchairs, nursing dolls or playing with toys. One could not fail to be impressed with the excellence of the accommodation and equipment of the school, and under the supervision of the head teachers (Mr. W. Mason and Miss Taylor) everything seems to work most smoothly. After watching the children at their lessons, the visitors were next able to see them at play, for an adjournment was made to tho school yards where organized games were soon in fall swing. These too are a new J feature of school life, for instead of the youngsters j rushing about with no particular object in view, they are all definitely occupied in some game. They seemed thoroughly to enjoy the fun. A number of girls, daintily costumed, also entertained the visitors with ao maypole dance and a gipsy song and dance, though the heavy shower interfered with the festivities for a time. Altogether it was a most interesting afternoon, and parents and scholars alike will look forward to the next " Garden day" with much pleasure. The visitors included the Mayor and Mayoress and the Misses Smethurst.

INLAND CORRESPOIIDESCE.

The term "Inland Correspondence " means cor- respondence posted within the United Kingdom, including the Isle of Manand the Channel Islands. "Inland Correspondence " is divided into the following classes : (a) Letters (d) Newspapers b) Postcards (e) Parcels (c) Halfpenny pacliets Not only letters, but any document or article (with a few trifling exceptions) which can be trans- mitted by post at all, may be sent by letter post, the only limitation being that of size.

LE CT E-I2 POST. The prepaid rate of postage is as follows Not exceeding 4 ozs. in weight ... Id. For every additional 2 0z5.... I. A letter posted unpaid is chargeable on delivery with double postage; a letter insufficiently paid, with double the deficiency. No letter may exceed two feet in length, one foot in width, or one foot in depth.

, PosT-e inns. The prepaid rate of postage on every postkard is one half-penny, and on every reply post-card one penny. A post-card posted unpaid is chargeable on delivery with one penny. Cards used as post-cards must be rnade of ordinary card-board, not thicker than the material used for the thickest official post-card. They may not exceed ift 53. inches in length by 31 i es in width, or be less than 31 inches in length b inches in width. A gummed label (not to ceed 2 inches long and 2-inch wide) bearing the address may now be ailixed to the addrras side of card. If any of the rules relating to a post-card be infringed, the card will be treated as a letter. HALFPENNY PACKET POST. - . .

The Halfpenny Packet Post can be used only for packets not exceeding 2oz. in weight. Printed matter, &c., not in the nature of a letter, may be transmitted by this method. NEWSPAPER POST. The prepaid rate of postage on a registered news- paper, including any supplement thereto, whether posted singly or with others is /d. Newspapers not registered at the General Post 011 ice are treated in the post like any other printed matter.

PARCEL POST. The rates of postage on parcels area's follows: For a parcal .., not exceeding 1 lb. 0 3 „ exceeding 1 lb. 2 lb. 0 4 „ 2 lb. 3 lb. 0 5 PP 3 lb. 5 lb. 0 6 PP PP 5 lb. PP 7 lb. 0 7 99 7 lb. fP 8 lb. 0 8 IP PP 81b. PP 91b. 0 9 PP „ 9 lb. PP 10 lb. 0 10 10 lb. 11 lb. 0 11 No parcel may exceed 111 b. in weight. The size allowed for an inland parcel is : Greatestlength... 3 ft. 6 in. Greatest length and girth combined 6 ft. 0 in., For example—A parcel measuring 3ft. Gin. in its longest dimensions as much as 2ft. Gin, round its thickest part ; a short parcel may be thicker ; thus, if it measure no more than 3ft, in length, it may measure as much as 3ft. round its thickest part. • The postage on a parcel must be prepaid. Mark each parcel" Parcel Post." A parcel must not be posted in a letter box, but presented at the counter of a post office, and the sender should see that the weight, size and postage are in order before leaving. PARCELS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL). • Parcels are accepted for parcel post to most foreign countries under conditions similar to the inland regulations, except that for customs require- ments the contents mnst be declared. The customs charges can be prepaid or collected on delivery. The postage varies to different countries and must be prepaid. MONEY 02,DERS (INLAND.) The postal anthoritres cannot issue a single money Order for more than £4O, and will only cash them at the money order office at which they are made payable, unless they are crossed, when they can be paid through a bank. No fractional part of a Id. can be contnined in a money order. The rates of poundage are :—Not exceeding £l, 21. ; £3, 3d.; £lO, 4d.; £2O, 61. ; £3O, Bd. ; £4O, 10d, By paying an additional 21. and cost of the telegram of advice, a money order can be telegraphed under certain restrictions. MONEY ORDERS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL.) The maximum amount for which a money order i may be issued for places abroad varies n each particular place. The poundage rates are :—Not exceeding £l,3d. ; £2, Gd. ; and above that, 3d. for each additional £2 or portion of it. A fee of Gd. in addition to the ordinary poundage, together with cost of telegram of advice, enables money orders to ' be telegraphed to certain places abroad. POSTAL ORDERS. These are obtainable at any money order office in the United Kingdom, and possess the advantage over money orders that they can be mished at any money order office. If crossed, they can be paid into a bank. They are issued for fixed amounts, - rising by 6d., from 6d. to RI Is. The poundage fees are :—id. up to 2s. Gd.; Id. up to 155.; lid. up to 21s. Before parting with a postal order, always fill in the name of the person to whom the amount is to be paid. Each order is numbered, as is also the counterfoil attached, which latter should be retained and name of payee filled in. The Post- master-General will entertain no further claim after an order is once paid. Stamps to the amount of sd. can be affixed to make up odd sums. TELEGRAMS (INLAND). The Postmaster-General possesses4ilmost entirely, the privilege of transmitting,collecfang and deliver- ing telegrams in the United Kingdom. The charge for a telegram is a minimum amount of Gd., which covers 12 words, 'and an additional Id. /or each extra word. This charge includes delivery within the postal district if sent out for delivery from a head telegraph office, but if from a sub-office then within three miles only, beyond which a charge of 3d. per mile is made from the office door. All charges are, as far as possible, prepared by affixing stamps to telegram form. Address of person receiv- ing a telegram has to be paid for, bnt sender's name if written on back of form need not be. Five figures count as one word. The cost of a reply may be prepaid. Telegrams can be repeated on payment of half the original charge, which extra payment is refunded if error is detected. Telegrams may be posted in wall or pillar boxes, or banded to rural postmen, and are wired as soon as received at the nearest telegraph office. Late fees secure attention, in certain cases, to telegrams handed in after the usual hours. The cost of registering RD abbrevi- ated address, which must consist of two words, is £1 IS. TELEGRAMS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL) Must be written on special forms and are accepted in the language of any of the principal European countries. The rates vary, and are too numerous to detail here. POST OFFICE SAVINGS BANK. These are established at all money order offices. In ordinary cases the annual deposit must not exceed £5O, and the total amount £2OO. No person can have more than one account. Amounts placed in the bank on behalf of children under seven years of age cannot be withdrawn until the child reaches that age, and then only under his or her own signa- ture. The smallest amount received at a time is -Is., and this may take the form of 12 penny stamps affixed to a special form. Each depositor receives a bank book in which the amount of each deposit should be entered at the time of paying in. If the deposit is £1 or over, speoial acknowledgment is sent from the head London office. Interest is allowed at the rate of 24 per cent. Any amount up to and including £1 may be withdrawn without precious notice on presenting a bank book. The bank book should be sent each year, postage free, on the anniversary of the date when the account was opened, to the Controller of the Savings Bank Department for parposes of checking and adding interest. The withdrawal of meney can be expedited by telegraphing, the depositor paying cost of telegrams. P.O. TELEPHONE AND TRUNK LINE CHARGES. The foes for the use of the Trunk lines are as follows: For 25 miles or under ... 3d. PI 50 PI 17 t, 75 99 PP „ 100 „ every „additional 40 miles or fraction thereof... ... Gd. Between the hours of 7-p.m. and 7 a.m., six minutes conversation is allowed for the same price as three minutes between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m., and a reduced charge is made for three minute calls.

moTort CAR AND CYCLE REGULATIONS. Each one must be registered with the council of a county or county borough, the fee being £1 for a motor car, and ss. for a motor cycle. A registered number is assigned to each which it is an offence not to keep allixed whoa &lying. Each driver must possess a license, costing 55., to ho renewed every 12 months, and obtainable from the county authorities, which may be endorsed or suspended for reckless driving or certain other offences. The highest speed at which a car may be driven on the public highways is 20 wiles an hour, which is reduced to 10 miles under special local regula- tions. It is an offence under the Motor Car Act (1003), to drive a car in such a way on R pnblic highway as to be dargerous to the public, having regard to all the circumstances of the case. In the event of an accident to any person due to the presence of the motor car on the road, the driver must supply his name and address, and the owner and number of -tbe car, under heavy penal- ties. The driver must produce his "'leen-re at" the request of a pollee constable.

318 258 PRESENTATION OF A SILVER CUP.

Prior to the match Lady Greenell pfesented, on behalf of Sir Gilbert, a handsome silver cup to the I Works Association to be competed for in the annual handicap. Accompanying Lady Greenell were Mr. and Mrs. Robert Pierpoint,and there was a large attendance of howling enthusiasts. Mr. W. WEBSTER, a vice-president of the association, welcomed Lady Greenell, and said he did not need to remind those present of the interest which Sir Gilbert and her Ladyship took in all kinds of sport. They bad shown it many times both by word and deed. Lady GREENALT„ who was cordially received, said she had great pleasure in handing the trophy to Mr. Willett, chairman of the association. She regretted Sir Gilbert could not be with them that afternoon, as he was judging at the Buxton Show. Mr. WILLErr said the cup would he prized by the association, and the man who won it each year would, he had no doubt, treasure it during the time it was in his keeping. When the association started, ten or twelve works were affiliated with it. Now there were twenty, which supplied thirty teams. That showed that tits association was making progress, and they intended to go on improving. In conclusion Mr. Willet proposed a vote of thanks to Lady Greenall for her presence and and to Sir Gilbert for his generosity in presenting the cup. He added that Lady Ureenall had just promised him a cheque towards the proceeds that afternoon—an announcement that was received -with considerable pleasure. Mr. A. E. Bar RDETT seconded the vote which was cordially passed. Mr. PlEuroixr replied.

div.head: FAT FOLKS AND SKIMMED MILK DIET.
div.p: FAT FOLKS AND SKIMMED MILK DIET.

Physicians who are " cruel only to be kind" often prescribe a diet of skimmed milk for the reduction of fat. It may be ame but is certainly an insupport- able method of cure. Other doctors, more success- fully, and with mote consideration for their patient's comfort, prescribe a dessertspoonful after meals and at bedtime of the folloy-ing•: One half-ounce of Marmola, on ounce of fluid extract of Glycyrrhiza 8.P., one ounce of pure Glyceline B.P , and Pepper- mint Water to make six ounces in all, which is just 'as sure and quick a means of cure as any old- fashioned method could be., and a far more pleasant one, for a person can eat the same variety and quan- tity of. food as usual while taking this remedy and still lose twelve to sixteen ounces of superfluotit flesh a day.

div.head: BOWLING.
div.p: BOWLING.
SCOTTISH NATIONAL EXHIBITION.

With the Exhibition now considerably more than half-way through its career, there is every indication • that given reasonably flue wei.ther it will prove one of mmit successful enterprises of its kind that has ever taken place in Scotland. The public support, as shown by the high average of the daily attendance, is the best comnlinient that could le paid to the management, which has shown itself Very ready to provide special attraction for its patrons. A big scheme of illuminating the buildings is now being installed, and as soon as complete an inauguration ceremony will beheld when the lights will be spontane- ously switched on. Future events include a great Scots I gathering when contests will take place in the national I games a Marathon race from Linlithgow to Edinburgh, a distance of about 16 miles, and a grand Military Tournament. The latter which will be held on October 7th, Bth, oth, and 10th, is being organised by Col. Sir Robert Cranston, E.C.V.O. It has a strong list of supporters inducing T.U.H. the Duke and Prince of Connaught, Air. Haldane, Secretary for War, Duke of Argyll, Earl of Rosebery, and General Eir John French. Regiments already announcid ito take part include the Royal Field Artillery, Royal Scots Greys, Seaforth Highlanders, and the Lothians and Border Horse. The proceedings each day will terminate with a great military Tattoo in the evening.
