div.head: BOROUGH ?FINANCE. -- BOW THE RATEPAYERS' MONEY IS
div.p: BOROUGH ?FINANCE. -- BOW THE RATEPAYERS' MONEY IS
SPENT.

The Borongh Treasurer (Mr. John Fairhurst, F.S.A.A.), has just issued his annual abstract of the accounts of the Corporation of Warrington for the year ended 31st March last. The volume comprises 169 pages and gives a mass of valuable information as to how the ratepayers' money is expended. TUE BALANCE SHEET—W'ARRINGTON'S INDEBTEDNESS.

Accompanying the accounts is an aggregate balance Statement of the liabilities and assets of the Corpora- tion on the 31st March last. The total liabilities are set forth as amounting to £1,303,739 Os. 21. and the assets to £1,785,303 Os. Old., leaving an excess of assets of £481,503 19s. lOW. The balance sheet shows the liabilities and assets in connection with the following funds :
Property, Assets and Outlay. s. U.
Liabilities. £ s. d.

- Borough Rate 73,25-3 18 0 143,640 710 Improvement Rate ' 330,046 13 0 454,699 9 2 Sewers Rate . 39,152 9 4 75,101 13 0 Pimento and Library Education Beddleton Scholarship Parr Ran Private Improvement Expenses 15,083 13 0 15,083 10 0 Gas Works 181,954 3 1 307,163 10 7i Water Works 409,617 511 459,012 2 3 Electricity 93,135 8 1 109,048 9 4 Tramways Fire Engine Renewal rford & Wilderspool Causeways 573 5 11 Police Superannuation 16.255 0 9 Walker's Gift --
COST OF TEE POLICE FORCE.

The Watch Department's expenditure totalled £7,928 6s. ld.,and exceeded the receipts by £4059 10s. 4d. The largest item is for constable's wages. which absorb £5,714 6s. Id. In addition a sum of £l3B 10s. sd. was paid as boot allowance, and £6B ss. allowance in lieu of uniform. Clothing and accoutrements cost £333 Ils 3d., and a year's medical attendance on constables cost .119 16s. The expenditure on the maintenance of prisoners whilst in the Bridewell was £3B is., while the sum of £lOO Ils. 3d. was paid for the conveyance of prisoners. Maintenance of the buildings, &c., cost £2BO 16s. 11d., and there are payments to the Electricity Department for electric light and fittings to the amount of £Ol ss. 2d. The receipts in this department include £3,348 lie. 6d., being the Exchequer contribution of one-half the charge for pay and clothing of police. His Majesty's Paymaster-General contributes £lOl 4s. 10d. for the conveyance of prisoners to gaol. The propor- tion of fines and penalties imposed by the Borough Justices and handed over to this account was £B3 19s 3d., to which must be added £l2 ss. 61. for fees. The regis- tration of motor vehicles and licences for driving brought in £54 25.. while £lOl 7s. 9d. was received for special duty of police. THE CEMETERY.

- --- In the Cemetery Department gardeners'and labourers' wages amounted to £563 10s. and there was a sum paid to the Highway Department and for repairs to build- ings &c., of £76 4s. 3d. The burial fees paid to the clergy during the year were as follows :—Rector of Warrington, £46 7s. ; Vicar of St. Paul's, £25 7s. 23. ; Vicar of Holy Trinity, £ll 4s, 10d. ; Vicar of St. liarnabas', £l2 ss. Gd. ; Vicar of St. Peter's, £23 78.6 d.; Vicar of St. Ann's' ' 123 6s. 23. • Vicar of St. James', £lO 16s. 4d.; total £152 14s. 6d. The receipts included £366 3s. for purchased graves and £136 17s. for common or nnbought graves. Fees charged after first interment amounted to £257 Ss. and for excavating £293 ss. 6d. The total income amounted to £1,529 10s. Bd. and after deducting expenses there is a credit balance of £335 16s. 83.

TOWN HALL, PARK'S AND BATHS. In the Town Hall Department, hall keeper's and cleaners' wages totalled £236 11s. 2d. and maintenance of buildings, furniture and repairs is put down at £206 7s. Gd. In the Parks Department £7ll Is. id. was disbursed in gardeners', labourers', and park-keepers' wages. £65 119. 11d, has been spent on trees, plants and seeds and £27 4s. id. on food for birds and fishes. A contribution of £7O has been made to the Bands Association. There is an item of £ll9 12s. 4d. for greenhouse and .£97 15s. 4d. for demolishing greenhouse and erecting shelter. Maintenance of buildings, Ste., cost £lOl 16s. 10d., and there was an expenditure on £l4 135. 10d. on the public bowling greeo, Victoria Park, as well as £67 6s. for the caretakers' wages. The receipts from the green amounted to £45 us. 63. £2O Gs. 6d. was received for the hire of plants. In the Baths Department the chief item of expenditure was £317 14s, 4d. for superintendent's and assistants' wages. The cost of fuel was £l4B lls. 11d, and the water bill was £133 his. 6d. Soap and cleaning materials accounted for £52 17s. and £ll 7s. 23. was expended on maintenance of buildings and fittings. Receipts from bathers totalled £521 17s. Bd., while the Education Department paid £5O for the use of baths for scholars. The total income was £535 2s. Id., and the expenditure was £1,013 2s. Od., so that the baths cost the ratepayers during the year £123 Os. 83. RIVERS DEPARTMEMT AND GYMNASIUM'.

The Rivers Department has spent £335 12s. 10d., the chief item being £229 15s. 81. for men's time watching sluices at Walton. The salary of Mr. Schofield Jack son, river surveyor, absorbed £l2O. The total expenditure in the Gymnasium Depart- ment was £322 15s. Id., and the receipts amounted to £197 7s. 11d., thus costing the ratepayers £125 7s. 2d. The largest item of income was £ll4 3s. 4d. from the! Education Department for use of room and salary of Instructor, while class fees totalled, 248 15s 01., and , penny class £0 Os. Bd. FINANCE DEPARTMENT. The salaries in the Town Clerk's oMce amounted to £1,459 us. •, Borough Treasurer's Department, £2,500 17s. 83. ; Borough Surveyor's °face, £1,402 Is. 2d. ; Clerk to the Borough Justices (including certain expenses), £538 Os. 6d. The amount paid on sinking fund totalled £1,839 7s. 10d. and the expenditure also included £2,653 6s. 9d. for interest on loans and £1,667 13s. 4d. on the Education Account, being the amount included in precept on overseers. COUNTY AND OTHER CHARGES.

The County charges totalled £2,036 14s. 10d. and included £1,613 13s, 10i. to Lancashire Asylums Board, £64 us. 3d. for maintenance of vagrant lunatics, and £Bl Is. 11d. to Lancashire Inebriates Act Board. Under the heading of exchequer contribution account there was an expenditure of £7,310 10s. ld. This includes a payment of £1,618 10s, Dd. to the Guardians of the Warrington Union for proportion of salaries of Union officers and medical appliances, and £1,015 17s. 21, for maintenance of pauper lunatics. The income on this account was £7,053 10s. 2d. GENERAL PURPOSES. THE SHIP CANAL LITIGATION.

In the General Purposes Department the expenditure totalled £3,124 14s. Bd. The largest item is £1498 Os. 6d. for professional services and expenses of witnesses &c., re action against Manchester Ship Canal Company. Coats and charges re action Edelsten v Corporation *mounted to £l5l is. Ocl. ; expenses of deputations, .£75 175.; printing, stationery and books, £3BB is. 7d.; Warrington Infirmary, a year's subscription £lO 10s. ; Museum and Library Fund, grant for branch libraries. .£139 7s. sd. : Warrington Distress Committee grant, £2OO ; rent of open spaces, £95 17s. Bd. ; maintenance Fcc,, of same, £lO6 3s. 9d. ; proportion of expenses incurred in carrying out the provisions of the Registra- tion of Voters Act, 1890, for the year 1906-7, £ll7 Bs. sd. ; municipal and auditors' elections expenses £l5B ss. lid. The income in the General Purposes Department was £233 132. 10d., leaving a deficit of .£3,191 Os. Md. PROFITS ON THE MARKETS. Once mole the markets prove a very profitable source of revenue, the total receipts being £5,610 7s. 33. Of this sum £4,216 14s. 6d. was derived from fair and market tolls, £299 17s. 6d. for rent of shops in th Market Hall, £B3l 17s. 4d. for rents of shops and stallY in market sheds, and £9O 15s. sd. receipts from lavatories. The expenditure amounted to £2190 2s. 3d. leaving a profit of £3,429 ss.od. A year's scavenging of the markets cost £260 and maintenance of buildings and stalls accounted for £95 2s. 2d. The Weights and Measures Department received £253 lls. Sd., and expended £2Ol 13s. 7d. ; expenses of deputation to London re Weights and Measures Conference amounting to £2l 2s. 93. and to Smethwiek re new regulations under Weights and Measures Act, 1904, to £5 12s. Gd. HOSPITAL AND HEALTH DEPARTMENT.
' t‘ll4l

The income of the Hospital Department amounted-to £431 19s. Gd. ho Newton-in-Makerflelcl Urban District Council paid r. 306 10s. 10d.for use of hospital and main- tenance of patients and the Warrington Rural District Council £lll 12s. 7d. The expenses of this department amounted to £3,113 Os. Bd. and in addition the small-pox hospital expenses totalled .Cll7 Is. 4d. Matron's, nurses' and servants' wages at the borough hospital absorbed £613 15s. 10d and hospital keepers' and gardeners' wages amounted to £266 13s. Bd. There was an expendi- ture of £362 2s. 9d. on provisions. In the Health Department notification of infectious diseases cost- .£7ll6s. 6d, and bacteriological ekaminations 245 7s. 6d. The expenses of depnatrons to Douglas re Royal Institute of Public Health amounted to £7 17s. Bd.; Bradford, re lodging houses, £3 19s. 6d. ; London re electrolytic disinfectant plant, £6 9s. ; London re Coe- ference on Infantile Mortality, £lB 9s. ; London re International Congress on School Hygiene, £5 6s. 7d. ; London re National Union of Public Health Authorities, £1 3s. ; attending meetings of Manchester Port Sanitary Authority £6.

div.head: COST OF SANITARY WORE.
div.p: COST OF SANITARY WORE.

In the Sanitary Works Department the expenses in connection with the Longford Manure Works totalled .£3,900 Is. 4d. Extensions during the year cost £723 13. Id, The intercepting depots cost .C 736 Bs. 2d.; nightsoil collection department, £7,667 49. 4d.;
scavenging department, £3,706 193. Bd. The sale of concentrated manure brought in £3,744 13s. 4cl.
THE HIGHWAYS. Highway work in Warrington daring the year cost £15,570 us. 9d. ; the receipts, largely for doing work for other Corporation departments, totalling £9,809 14s. 10d.

div.head: FIRE ENGINE.
div.p: FIRE ENGINE.

The expenses in this department amounted to .2818 4s. 9d., firemen's wages absorbing £379 Bs. 7d., and clothing and accoutrements £62 Us. 3d. The receipts from insurance companies and others as proportion of fire expenses amounted to £l9l 93. 10d. , STREET DIPROVENIENT AND LIGHTING.

- --- The amount paid to the Gas Department for a year's lighting of the streets and removal of lamps was £5,113 Is. lid., and to the Electricity Department £642 15s. 11. d. Purchases of land, Sm., and compensation in Folly Lane cost £133 16s. ; Friars' Gate, £7 ; Knuts- ford-road, .£4 103. 7d. Trees, guards, .54c. and planting trees accounted for £52 Os. Id. On the Street Improvement Loan Account the purchase of land and property, including costs, com- pensation Sc., in Barbauld-street, cost £3 15s. ; Butter- market-street, £3,537 103. ; Croppers Brow, £416 ss. ; Knutsford-road, £1,125 15s. ; School Brow, £450. BRIDGE-STREET IMPROVEMENT. - -

Under this head £59 Ils. 9d., was paid in valuers' fees; £l2 2.3. Gd. in Parliamentary agents' fees ; £2,995 153. for the purchase of chief rent and costs ; £1,750 for the erection of shops. The receipts were £1,923 lOs by re-sale of land. MUSEUM AND LIBRARY.

ut The expendite in connection with these institutions was £1,688 188. 4d., including £677 Os. 9d. on wages and salaries, £9l 14s. 93. for specimens, mounting, &c., £165 O. id. for books, £73 16s. 7d. for periodicals, £5O Os. 11d, for binding, and £B3 16s. 11d, for replace- ment of worn-out books. On- the branch libraries the outlay was £lOl 17s. Iod. The chief source of income was £6l 16s. fines paid by borrowers. This department receives the proceeds of a 116. rate (91,491 95.) and a special grant of .9139 7s. si. for branch libraries, with which to carry on its work, and it has ended the year with a balance in hand of £2ll 2s. 83. THE COST OF EDUCATION.

Elementary education in the Borough has during the year cost £38,121 73., the largest item of expenditure being £28,234 7s. Ild, on teachers' salaries. The salaries of officers other than teachers amounted to £1,723 Ss. 10d., books and apparatus cost £1,3809a., fuel, light and cleaning £2,475 53., repairs to buildings £33045. 7d., garden at 13amont school £56 Ss. Gcl. The amount raised from tho Barough Rate for elementary education was £13,397 10s. 10(1., and grants from Board of Education totalled £24,636 ISs. 9d. School fees brought in £2,231 13s. 2d. On higher education the expenditure was £7,521105.11d., including £1,529 9s. 10d. for salaries of teachers at the ,1 Secondary school and Pupil Teachers' Centre and £2,098 Bs. 2d.for salaries of teachers at evening schools. Salaries of officers other than teachers totalled £259 9s. Sd. The ratepayers contributed £3,271 2s. 6d. to this department. and grants from the Board of Education totalled £2,453 12s. Bd. The fees amounted to £626 15s. Under the Education capital account there has been paid during the year in respect of the erection &c.o f the Beamont Council School £1222 17s. Gd. and in respect of the Bolton School .£7,4 t 0 13s. 7d. The Middletoh Scholarship fund shows an expenditure of £2l lls. 51. on school fees and materials and there is a balance to be oarried• forward of £l9B Is. Id.

div.head: PARR HALL PROFITS.
div.p: PARR HALL PROFITS.
Twelve months' profit on the Parr Hall amonnted to £l3l 3s. 4d., the amount paid for the use of the hall being £730 17s. 11d. There is a bad debt of £22 ls.lod. POLICE SU PEEtANNITATIO

The Police Superannuation Fund at date amounts to £1,25 Os. 93. The money is invested in the Warring- ton, Manchester, Bolton, St. Helens and Stockport Cor- porations. Pensions have been paid during the year amounting to £516 15s. 83. SIR PETER WALRER'S GIFT.
The balance in hand on this account amounts to VSII 15s. Id. There has been no expenditure during the year.
GAS WORKS PROFIT.

The gas works account shows that the gross profit for the year amountisd to £3,500 12s. 3d. From this must be deducted the amount paid for one year's annuities, interest and sinking fund, amounting to £8,207 12s. 4d., the sum paid to the relief of rates from the previous year's profits £ll,OOO.

div.head: WATERWORKS.
div.p: THE WATERWORKS.

The gross profit on the water undertaking amounted to £16,711 18s. 7d. Payments for interest and annuities absorbed £13,221 7s. Gd., and sinking fund £4,567 15s. Gd. ; the balance in hand at the end of the year being £2,939 Os. 7d. The principal expenditure is under the following heads :—Management account, £1,832 Os. id. ; Winwick pumping station, £1,512 Os.; Houghton Green pumping station, £909 ss. Gd. ; Appleton reServoir, £212 13s. ; repairs to mains, Scc. £1.263 Ss. ; rents, rates, taxes, &c., £2,801 us. 4d. • lfittings, £796 Os. sd.

div.head: L.kWSON &RBITRATION.
div.p: L.kWSON &RBITRATION.

The Waterworks capital account gives the following particulars of the expenses re Lawson Arbitration : Costs, fees, &a., £1,702 16e. div.head: DAYLIGHT SAVING.
div.p: DAYLIGHT SAVING.
Later Sunsets During Summer.

To TITE EDITOR OF THE WESTMINSTER GAZETTE.] Sir,—[ have found it very difficult to get people to clearly understand how the change during April to September would work if the " Daylight Saving " Bill should pass. After much trial of words to shortly express the matter, it appears to me that the following sentence hits the mark exactly : " The sun will set an hour later than it does now." Thus, to-day (August 25th) the almanscks give the time of sunset as 7.3 p.m. If the Act had already come into force the time of sunset would be 8.3, and the almanacks would have been printed so. This would have been brought about simply by clocks having been 'I pat forward an hour on a specified day in April last. 1 lam just off for my fortnight's holiday • 1 should be i very glad if the time of sunset was not till about eight I o'clock just now instead of about seven o'clock as it is. 1 There would be no "getting up earlier," no alteration in the times of trains, meals,Scc., but simply " the time of sunset and sunrise is an hour later during summer than before the Act was in force."—Yours faithfully, LOVER OF DAYLIGHT.

div.head: LEAP BEFORE A TRAIN.
div.p: LEAP BEFORE A TRAIN.
Warrington Man's Serious Injuries.

A sensation was caused at the Earlestown Railway Station at about nine o'clock on Thursday morning, when a man named William Claltit is alleged,attempted to commit suicide by jumping in front of a train. CIO, who is a Warrington man, living in Slater Street, had been spending the night in Earlest own with his brother-in-law, and the latter accompanied him to 1,4 station this morning on his return home. Whilst waiting for the train, a Manchester train approached the station and Clan, it is said, took a sudden leap in front of the engine. When picked up he was found to have had all his fingers, on both hands, and one of his feet crushed to a I pulp. He had had a miraculous escape from instant death. ' He was placed in the 9.10 train to Warrington, and upon arrival was conveyed on an ambulance to the infirmary, where his fingers had to be amputated. lie is now in a serious condition. 1

The people do not believe the book of Genesis, therefore they do not believe in the structure that has been erected by ignorance and a desire to explain the unknown. For myself I am satisfied that that there is no more need for " Atheistic hash" to be given out at the street corner. Ministers in their churches do all that is necessary in this direction. Socialism may be treated in the same fashion. Science that is conquering the air is also revolutionising the conditions of life on land and water. The resources of civilization are not exhausted, nor are some of the sayings of the good old Book a dead letter. He that will nat work, neither shall he eat. The time has now come when my employer mast recognize my brotherhood. He must clearly understand that the proletariat of the world, if Christian, will demand that the Fatherhood of God be no longer fiction, but an actual, Practical fict. If atheistical, he will have to deal with reason, and the reasonable man's advice will be, put your ear to the ground and listen. Ifq have cleared the ground, and proved to my Christian friend that the Bible does not, as at present interpreted, Meet the requirements of the twentieth century, I may go to the next step in the ascent of man. Man was not primarily born to sin and reared in iniquity. Neither is man that is born of woman, full of misery, as I recently heard a preacher at a graveside state. In an old Bible I have the date of creation is given as 4,001 years ago. At that time Onions and civilizations were fading into the past. Christians talk of eternity as if the idea of eternity could be grasped; as if it pertained only to the future and not to the past. Man is ascending, and the explanation is the answer to the question: Why? to be dealt with further.
H. IVHITHAIT.

div.head: WHY? WHY?
div.p: WHY? WHY?

[BY MR. HENRY WHITHAI.II. • A few weeks ago the " Britth Weekly" contained an article, written by As editor, Dr. Nicoll, the heading to which was somewhat like the above demand, "Why?" I simply borrow it and emphasising it, try, as is my duty, as it is that of every other man, to work out an explanation. I would like every man and woman to read the article. It deals with the one question that most certainly lies at the root of all our , trouble, and must not be answered by the mere assertion that " civilization is a failure." No, as Mr. Gladstone once said, the resources of civilization are not yet exhausted. I will give a few of the Doctor's questions : Why is it that virtue is clad in rags and vice wears purple? That those who are a curse to mankind flourish and grow, while those whose whole life is for the blessing of the race travel their journey with hardly one ray of sunshine ? Why is it that the march of progress is so miserably impeded? Why is it that when a step in advance is made after infinite endurance and hazard, there comes a reaction which makes it doubtful whether any ground has been won at all? Why is it that the curse of war still exists, and that the prospect of its end is so dark and doubtful? The above are merely a few of the searching questions the Doctor puts before his readers. Going on he says, "Almost every long life is fall of difficulties that lacerate the heart and perplex the mind. Faith is daunted and exercised in a thousand ways. We stood the other day by the new-made grave of a girl who died at the moment when a happy betrothal was

ripening into marriage." Leaving the doctor, allow me to give a litt'e of my recent experience. A couple of months ago, as a convalescent, I was ordered by my doctor to seek change of air in the Sierra Nevada mountains. Harms a married daughter whoss home was in an old mining camp of the Sierras, I pitched my tent there for a couple of months; some three to four thousand feet above sea _level. While vast pine

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Cricket.

Local enthusiasts naturally took some interest in the match between Esrlestown and St. Helens Rees, which was played at Newton on Saturday to decide who should be the holders of the West Lancashire championship for the next twelve months. The game was well worth seeing, and the fortunes of the contestants fluctuated to such an extent that excitement always ran high. In the end,how- ever,the Recs.were triumphant by a margin of three with three wickets to spare. Earlestown had first turn at the wicket, but Gregory and Gray bowled with such effect that all were dismissed for EL The Recs ' men, however, made a poor show at the start, and were tumbled out at a rapid rate by Unsworth. It was to Captain Norman Pilkington's display that the Recs. ; owed their ultimate success. Going in first, he success- fully battled with the bowling throughout, and carried ; out his bat for an excellent 35.

Mr. James Dodds, the President of the League, witnessed the match, and at the close he presented the cup and medals to the victors. The trophy has not had to travel far this time, for St. Helens were the cham- pions last season and, next to winning themselves,would no doubt be most pleased at the success of their neigh- bours, the Recs.

In the course of a short speoch,Mr. Dodds said that he was very sorry he arrived so late, as the St. Helens team had lost two wickets for four runs when he arrived, but he was pleased to see the strenuous struggle the team made later, and finally emerge successful from a glorious contest. It only went to show what a great game cricket was, and if only a teem worked well together what good resulted. He also referred to the late Colonel R. Pilkington, and commended his honour- able principles to those assembled, and said how sorry he was that the county and this part of Lancashire especially had lost a most loyal man. He was proud of the fact that Mr. Norman, son of the late colonel, was captain of the Recs, team, and paid a very high tribute to the game he had played. He then presented the cup to the Rena. captain, who said how proud he was to be able to receive that beauti- ful cup, and hoped that the League would still be carried on as it had been, and that all the clubs would still fight honourably and well to earn the distinction that the Recs. had done. He also thanked Mr. Dodds for the kind words he had said of his father. Mr. Marsh also spoke on behalf of the Earlestown team.

Warrington were at home on Saturday and recorded a well-deserved victory at the expense of Ashton-under- Lyne. The game was sternly fought and it was only sheer pertinacity when the odds were against them,that gained Warrington the honours. Only nine runs separ- ated the teams. Warrington had flist innings and,, amassed 100, J. W. Bainbridge distinguishing himself with a dashing display for 34 ; while W. H. Podmore made 15.

The visitors exerted every effort to win, and good displays by G. Radcliffe (23) and W. B. Howarth (24) Put them in cheerful spirits. Creswell was responsible for the sudden termination of the game. After he had bowled Booth in his first over, he dismissed Hollister and Watson with successive balls, and Ashton's chances had gone. Ins analysis worked out at 5 wickets for 20 runs.
Warrington 2nd drew with Ashton-under-Lyne 2nd, the game being notable for a splendid display by P. B. Hawtln who made 43.

St. James's continue their victorious career in the Warrington and District League competition and on Saturday they defeated Walker's Brewery without much difficulty. Minards batted well for 16 not out and Holt was in great form with the ball, taking six wickets for five runs.

The Junior Leaguers were busy, Orford triumphing over Lovely-lane by the narrow margin of 2 runs after a most exciting match, and Marsh House-lane sending St, James's Juniors to the rightabout. Mann and Carman bowled with deadly effect, taking five wickets for nine runs and four for 12 respectively.
Walker's Brewery eleven have had a good season and now stand at the top of the Manchester and District Brewery League,thus becoming the holders of the shield and medals.

Sankey Wire Mills gave a good account of themselves at Hough Green where they ran up a majority of 45. W. Woodcock (23) and J. Hawthorn (19) were the top scores and A. B. Miles bowled in fine style, taking eight wickets for five runs.
Grappenhall 2nd entertained Lyrnm 2nd and were victorious by 37. Scoring ruled low, F. Robinson beading the list with 12, while J. Mottram knocked up

div.head: Bowling.
div.p: Bowling.

The chief lonl event on Saturday was the charity match between the %Warrington and Eccles works associations. The members of the bowling fraternity are willing to do their share in aiding deserving causes and the proceeds of Saturday's match will enable them to hand over a fair sum to the Infirmary and District Nursing Association. As for the match, it was com- pletely satisfactory from the %Warrington point of view, the home trundler winning by 90 points.

One of the most interesting games was that between W. Patrick, the hardworking secretary of the Wsrring- ton Association, and G. B. Hurst. The Eccles man was the first to get going and had a lead of 4-1. Patrick, however, soon equalized matters and the players peeled at 4, C, 7, 8 and 11. Hurst then gained a single but Patrick was on the alert and they were once more level at 14. Patrick then bowled the winning wood and gained a popular and well-deserved victory.

The redoubtable G. BAH had a very easy task, his opponent—S. Davies—only getting two points. G. Ball, jun., who captained the Warringtonians, had the satisfactiou of bettting the visiting captain (W. Swipe) by 15-7.

Prior to the match there was an interesting little ceremony, Lady Greenall, on behalf of Sir Gilbert, presenting a silver cup to the Warrington Association for competition in the annual handicap.—Mr. J. Willett, chairman of the Association, accepted the trophy, and was able to give some gratifying information as to the success of the association.
The first round of tbe annual handicap will he cora- pleted to-day. A list of the games will be found in another column.

There was a keen struggle between Penketh Tannery and Ilighfield Tannery on the Highfleld Green,the visitor's triumphing by a single point. St. Paul's Warrington, visited Altrincham and tried conclusions with St. George's Church House. They did not give a very good account of themselves, the home team being successful in the singles by 33 points and in the doubles by 15 points.

Bowlers connected with the Lancashire and Cheshire I I County Amateur Association will be pleased to hear that there is a likelihood of a match being arranged between the °leave family, of Warrington, and a family of bowlers from Mossley Hall. The challenge comes from Joe Harrison, of the Old Ship, who with his six sons and grandson, would like to mat the Gleave family on any independent green for the honour claimed I Playing in a recent final at Warrington were father and four sous of the Weave family, whilst assisting the other team was W. Weave, a cousin.

div.head: Cycling.
div.p: Cycling.

Much dicapnointraent was felt by the members of the Warrington Club on Saturday last, when the annual fishing match had to be postponed, owing to the poison- ous state of the water at Little Leigh, the venue for the day. The contest has however been arranged to take place at Bollington this afternoon, in lieu of the visit to Chester' and a good muster of anglers is confidently expected to put in an appearance at this convenient spot. Those unable to proceed by road, will leave by the 2-26 train from Bank Quay, to Dunham Massey.
The first mid-week run of the season took place on Tuesday evening, only a small number braving the elements, which were anything but conducive to cycling.
Wednesday evening at Sankey saw the remaining consolation games played, in what has been a highly successful handicap.
The riding season, which is now nearing its close will conclude with a bowling handicap at Sankey, to be followed by a distribution of prizes won by the mem- bers during the season.
Water Polo.

The Warrington polo team played Atherton, the leaders of the Manchester and District League, in a friendly match lit Atherton on Tuesday evening. The visitors defended the shallow end in the first half and soon scored through C. Ashton, who registered another goal a short time after. The homesters now scored but the visitors sent the ball through the net again and the score at the interval was Warrington 3 goals, Atherton 1.

In the second half Warrington were the first to again score and the game looked like a walk over for them but the home team rallied and scored 3 goals in as many minutes, this bringing the teams level. Atherton however, scored the winning goal and the final arrived Atherton 5, Warrington 4.
The return match will be played on September 17th when the losers should have no difficulty in avenging their narrow defeat.

div.head: LOCAL WEDDINGS.
div.p: LOCAL WEDDINGS.

Clarke—Stanworth. There was a pretty wedding at Holy Trinity Church on Thursday afternoon when Mr. George Clarke, son of Mrs. Shaw, of Wilderspool, was married to Miss Eleanor Florence Stanworth, daughter of Mrs. Sudlow, of Priestley-street. The Vicar (Rev. E. C. E. Carleton) officiated. The bride, who was given away by her brother, Mr:' Harry Stanworth, was attired in a beautiful empire gown of cream Shantung silk and gold embroidered lace; She wore a helio crinoline hat covered with flowers and feathers, and carried a beautiful bouquet of sweet peas. The bridesmaid was Miss May Sudlow, who wore a dress of white Jap silk and white crinoline hat with a ostrich feather. Her bouquet was composed of sweet peas. The duties of best man were discharged by Mr. A. White. At the conclusion of the service the" Wedding March" was played by the -organist, Mr. Randall. The wedding breakfast was served at Atkinson's Caf6, Bridge- street, many guests being present. Numerous hand- some presents were received. Collier-Rowson. There was a large congregation at the Dunstable Priory Church on Monday morning, when Mr. Kenneth , A. Collier, eldest son of Mr. Aubrey Collier, of the Bank House, Dunstable, was married to Miss Winifred Rovrson, youngest daughter of the late Mr. Richard Byrth Howson, of Victoria ouse, Wilderspool, War- rington. The wedding wasla quiet, but very pretty one, and although taking pla e at a rather early hour, the bride and bridegroom are both well-known and much liked in Dunsdale, hence the large con- gregation of friends and well-wishers. The Rector (Rev. W. W. C. Baker) officiated, assisted by the Rev. A. G. Hodgson (curate) The bride, who was given away by her brother' Mr: R. H. Howson, of Frodshatn, Chester, was attired in her travelling dress, which was an Empire gown of pastel blue chiffon cloth, trimmed with Oriental passementerie, with vest and sleeves of pretty ivory net.. The kat was of cream net, trimmed with wisteria of a pastel shade. Her bouquet , was a beautiful combination of white carnations and heather, and was the gift of the bridegroom. The duties of best man were carried out by Mr. Brough W. Girling, of Hertford. At the conclusion of the serviceihe ' Wedding March" was played by the organist, Mr. H. Deacon, and the bells rang out a merry peal. After the ceremony, the wedding break- fast took place at the Bank House, only a few imme- diate relatives being invited. The honeymoon is being spent in the Channel Islands. The presents were very handsome and numbered 120, showing the great esteem in which Mr. " Ken " Collier and his bride are held. Their future residence will be at West Hill-road, Luton. Benning—Rowson. ..

forests stretched away to the distant horizon the v-iew was grand beyond my powers of description. Here, it seemed to me was peace, and above all health. Surely the strife and crime that has made San Francisco notorious the world over would never dare to enter this paradise. I was mistaken. Although but a small hamlet of about 200, I had to say before I left it that I had found, comparatively speaking, as much crime and sorrow as I should find in the city of half-a-million when I returned to it. My first acquaintance was with an old English lady who, with a daughter who seemed to be near the last stage of consumption, lived in a miserable old wooden shack further up in the moun- tains. Think of it ; these two, the mother at least SO and the daughter over 40, both helpless, and nearly penniless. I passed a number of hours with them, the two with only one thought, would the daughter recover from her sickness? This was the matter of our talk. I gave them the address of Dr. Allibone, of London, as a specialist on the white plague question. The last I saw of them they vere off to Colorado, two helpless, friendless things facing almost a week's journey to meet they did not know what. The next case was a consumptive born in the village, a man over 30. He had returned to his home about the same time as I landed in the town, and on the day he returned to his home, his mother aged seventy, while attending to her washing, fell and broke her arm. Before I left the son died ; I attended his funeral. Of misery brought on by drunkenness I could say a deal, and all about this small town of 200. I must speak of only one. The drunkard in this case is part owner of a nice little business in the shape of a gold mine. I had the pleasure, such as it was, of spending an evening with the children, throe boys and two girls. The eldest girl, about 12, is certainly one of the brightest and prettiest girls I ever met with. Her great sorrow is that on account of poverty she cannot go through the high school and so prepare herself to take charge of her younger brothers and sister. Where is the mother? Dead, she died two years ago, and the baby, just come into this strange world died shortly after. Why? There was a death bed scene ; when I heard it related the lump in my throat was a pretty large one. As she lay there dying, her children around her, and her husband somewhat sober, she cried out her last appeal "Oh Jack, Jack, if the Lord had only taken you instead of me, it would have been better for the children." My daughter knew the mother, whom it had pleased the Lord to take away, and tells me she was one of the best influences in the town. What I have related above of my own experience and of Dr. Nicoll's experience does, I think, justify me in saying it is time that the demanding question— Why ? should have an answer, if net from the Christian's spirit world, then from the Agnostic's, Rationalist's, or Atheistic's scientific world. For myself I have no hope that the Christian, as a Christian, AI ill ever give us the civilization that will make life worth living to those who are of the third and fourth generation. Mr. Balfour claims to he one with the Pan-Anglicans he addressed in the Albert Hall. Allow me to quote him. He said :—" For my own part I cannot con- ceive human society permanently deprived of the religious element. On the other band, I look to science far more than to the work of statesmen, to the creation of constitutions, to the elaboration of social systems, to the study of sociology. I look to science, and to science more than anything else, as the great ameliorator of the human lot. If I had to believe that these two powers were indeed immutably and perpetu- ally antagonistic then it would be impossible for me to avoid that hopeless despair which makes effort impos- sible, which deprives labour of all fruit for the future, whether we are living to see it accomplished or not, 'which makes the travail and struggle of mankind towards a better condition of society utterly beyond any reasonable expectation." Those who are at all acquainted with the writings of Mr. Balfour will, notwithstanding the above, know how narrow is the strip of ground that separates him from the late Mr. Bradlaugh and the late Mr.Holyoake. On science and science only must we depend if we are to keep clear of "hopeless despair." I have near me a pretty full report of the Pan- Anglican meetings recently held in London, and I have read most of it. I felt miserable pessimism running through the whole of it. Pessimism seems to tingle in the veins of Mr. Balfour as he looks upon the world and notes the mighty changes that come rapidly as moving pictures. I have just read the report of the 254th festival of the Sons of the Clergy Corporation and I find the sermon was preached by the Rev. the Hon. Edward Lyttleton, Headmaster of Eton. The Old Priory Church, Dunstable, was crowded with a large and fashionable congregation on Satur- day, August 16th, when the marriage was solemnized of Lieutenant Charles Stuart Banning, R.N., second son of Mr. C. C. S. Benning, Town Clerk of Dunstable, with Miss Effie Maud Rowson, daughter of the late Mr. R. B. Rowson, of Dunstable, and formerly of Victoria House, Wilderspool. Lieut. Benning was accompanied by five of his brother officers, in lull naval uniform, and these, contrasting with the beautiful dresses of the bride and her attendant maids, combined to make one of the prettiest spectacles ever witnessed in Dunstable's historic old Church. The service was fully choral, and was beautifully rendered. The Rector (Rev. W. W. C. Baker) per- formed the marriage ceremony, assisted by the Rev F. C. N. Hicks, Dean of Keble College, Oxford. The bride's dress was an exquisite gown of oyster shot satin, made in Empire style, ornamented with ' pearl mid crystal trimming and draped with real brussels lace. The train was suspended by a hand- some paste buckle, from either side of which were flowering panels of lace, attached to the gown with pearl and crystal trimming. The bridesmaids, Misses Monica, Doris and Penelope Benning (sisters of the bridegroom), and Miss Mary Healing, wore pretty " floral dresses, made in Empire style, with fichu bodices I trimmed with white silk lace and merve silk in pink and pale blue. A tiny page —Master Scott Baker, one of the Rector's sons--accompanied the bride as train- bearer. The bride was given away by Mr. Philip Champion, and Lieut. M. Brotherton, R.N., accompanied Lieut. Benning as best man. The groomsmen were: Lieut. H. D. Edwards, R.N., Lieut G. 'W. Naper, R.N., Lieut. M. E. Nasmith, R.N., and Lieut. M. 11. S. Macdonald, R.N. A reception was afterwards held at " The Limes," where upwards of 200 guests were entertained. A string band played on the lawn during the afternoon and evening. Later in the afternoon the happy couple left for London Ca l'ollte for Norway, where the honeymoon will be spent. On leaving " The Limes," Lieut. Brenning and his bade had to pass under the crossed swords of his brother officers, and again a merry peal from the Church belfry was rung. The bride's travelling dress was a pretty vieux rose silk taffeta gown, trimmed with gold and silk braid. Lieut. and rs. Banning's future residence will be at Dovercourt, Harwich.

div.head: PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING
div.p: PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING
SOCIETY.
First Annual Picnic.

Much interest was taken in the first annual picnic in connection with the Parliamentary Debating Society which was held on Saturday afternoon, between fifty and sixty members and friends journeying to Acton Bridge. The majority went by 'buses supplied by Mr. E. Connor; the remainder cycled. The weather during the morning was not at all promising, but as the after- noon turned out to be wonderfully line the drive through the well-wooded and, undulating country side was much enjoyed. Arriving at the Station Hotel, the pleasure-seekers spent the afternoon in sports. A capital programme had been arranged by Mr. W. Mason, the Clerk of the House, and entry forms had been distributed amongst the party en route. Some _excellent races were sees and there were many tight finishes, inches only separat- ing the winners. Mrs. E: Osborne and Mrs. T. Locker acted as judges and performed their arduous duties efficiently.

div.head: DETAILS OF SPORTS.
div.p: DETAILS OF SPORTS.

Old Boys' Handicap (over 40 years of age) ; distance ' 80 yards ; handicap, one yard for each two years.-1 Mr. E. England (Chancellor of the'Exchequer) ; 2, Mr ' Charles Phnston (the Speaker.) Youths' Handicap (under 40 years); 100 yards; same handidap as Old Boys' ; 20 years to be scratch man.-1, Mr. W. Mason (the Clerk of the House) ; 2, Mr. J. Howes, jun. (the Liberal Whip). _ Ladies' Precision Match in Accurate Aiming (no handicap or age limit).-1, Mrs. Healey ; 2, Miss Plinstou. - Flag Squadron Race (tie Council challenge his Majesty's Ministers.)—Ministers beat the Council. Scratch Three-legged Race, GO yards, each pair of competitors to consist of members of different parties. —l, Messrs Rathbone and Howard. Ladies' Walking Match, short distance.—Married ladies : 1, Mrs Lunt. Single ladies • 1, Miss Waywell. An excellent tea had been provided by Mr. Dallow, and promptly at 5.15 the party sat down. The Speaker took his place at the head, mad was supported by the Deputy-Speaker (Councillor Steel), the Premier (Mr. John Upson), the Leader of the Socialist party (Coun- cillor James Ball), the Clerk of the House (Mr. W. Mason), the Hon. Treasurers of the Picnic (Mr. P. H. Bennett and Mr. E. England), and the Hon. Secretary (Mr. Edmund Osborne). The vrovision was plentiful, and ample justice was done to at by the company, all of whom had acquired an engaging appetite from the drive—improved in many cases by the sports. After the prizes had been handed to the successfal athletes, the Hon. Secretary briefly expressed the pleasure of the members at seeing so many ladies present. He exhorted them to persuade their husbands, sweethearts and friends, if they were not already mem- bers, to join the society. It was very probable that a prominent member of Parliament would take part in the first debate of the next session (the last Thursday in September) and he hoped that the ladies would be present. The society was flourishing, and everything pointed to a very successful session. The party then adjourned whilst the tables were being cleared, some taking part in' the bowling match and others in the cricket match. The gentlemen, who had to bowl with their left hands, suffered befeat at the light hands (although one young lady was very proficient with her left) of the ladies. At 7.30 the party assembled to listen to a programme of music which had been prepared by Mr. ?Nat. Cook, jun. (the Deputy-Clerk of the House) and which was thoroughly enjoyed. After a vote of thanks, proposed by Councillor Ball (West Wolverhampton) and seconded by Mr. M. G. Hearne (South Kilkenny), to the artistes and the hon. secretary, the 'buses were loaded and the party com- menced the homeward journey. The evening was fine, • and Warrington was reached about eleven o'clock. The I first picnic was a great success and everybody spent a really good time.

div.head: MR. LLOYD GEORGE'S PORTRAIT.
div.p: MR. LLOYD GEORGE'S PORTRAIT.

SITS FOR SIR LUKE FILUES, R.A. The Chancellor of the Exchequer gave a sitting on Thursday morning, at his studio in Kensington, to Sir Luke Fildes, 8.A., who has been commissioned by the Incorporated Law Society to paint the right hon. gentleman's portrait for their hall. Mr. Lloyd George will be represented as wearing his Chancellor's robes.

div.head: WAR RINOTON COMPANY PROSECUTION.
div.p: WAR RINOTON COMPANY PROSECUTION.

At the Borough Police Court, yesterday, before ~t 1 Mayor and other magistrates, Henry Walter Griw director of the Lancashire Dental Institute, was eur monad for neglecting to send to the Board of Trade

annual return-and suininary for the year 1907. Mr. W. B. Forshaw prosecuted on behalf of the BoSi of Trade and Registrar of Joint Stock Companies, al said it had been suggested that in the case of privat companies there was no reason for requiring the rata He, however, contended that there was a very go°l reason—that the creditors and persons who were likel; to have dealings with a company should, if they desit be put into possession of the facts relating to it. W" regard to this case, in April the Registrar of Joint Si Companies sent notice that the return had not been f and warned the company that unless it was filed •wit' 14 days the default would be reported to the solicitor t` the Board of Trade and proceedings instituted. No no% was taken of the communication and on August 12, , notice was served on the defendant from the 0a91,1 solicitor to the Board that unless the return was within seven days proceedings would be taken. t" return, however, was not filed until August ith— day the summons was served. He understood that company ceased to carry on business about six Yebi ago, that it had no assets and no debts and to all ioteo and purposes was defunct. No steps, however, taken to have the company struck off the register , therefore the annual return was required. The it return was filed in 1907. Under the circumstances, the costs would he heavy (17) and defendant WOl.l, have to pay any fine that was inflicted out of his 0; pocket, Mr. Forshaw suggested that the magistral,, might take a lenient view of the case, as he intended report the matter to the Registrar and the coo3Pali would be taken off the lists. The Bench decided, in view of the fact that company would be struck a the register, tt: the case on payment of costs (t 7

MONKS, HALL & CO.'S RECREATION CLUB. ---- Flower Show and Sports. ---- The members of Messrs. Monks Hall and Co.'s Recreation Club were fortunate in selecting Saturday for their annual gala day. The weather was delightful and a large gathering was attracted to the recreation ground in Lovely-lane to see the flower show and sports which constituted the main features of the pro- gramme. Notwithstanding the difficulty of success- fully growing flowers and vegetables in ' smoky industrial neighbourhoods, the club has engendered a lively interest in horticulture among its members and the show on Saturday was exceedingly creditable. The exhibits were neatly arranged in k marquee and called forth general admiration. In the absence of Mr. F. W. Monks, the exhibition was opened by Mr. G. Bowman, ipresident of the club, Mr. Helsel' Owen presiding. Next week the polo team will be busy, matches being played with South Hill away on Wednesday and at St Helens at home on Thursday evening, both these fixtures being league matches. One of the attractions at Runcorn New Baths on Wednesday evening next (this being the occasion of the opening of the Baths) will be a water polo match between teams representing Warrington and Widnes. This should prove very enjoyable for the Runcorn people and will be the first polo match to be played in the town. Besides the St. Helens match on Thursday evening there will be a 50 yards schoolboy's race and owing to the great number of entries for this event, the Baths will be open at 7.30 to commence at 8 o'clock instead of 8.15. The result, of the draw for the semi-final of the Works Squadron Competition is as follows : White- cross v. Co-operative Stores, Post Office v. T. Allen and Sons, and Crosfleld's v. Corporation to be swam on September 17th. Rugby Football—Prospects for the Season. The annual eight months football campaign opens on Saturday next, and what with County Leagues, Northern Union League, South-West Lancashire League, Northern Union Cup, Lancashire and Yorkshire Cups, and an Australian visit the Northern Union clubs are in for a busy time. In all probability both players and spectators will have had enough before April 30th. likaiix months football season ought to be ample, VW the tendency seems to be to extend rather than shorten the period. Warrington open with a League match at Leigh, a fixture they won in handsome style last season. In fact the scores against Leigh were 28 —3 at Wilders- pool, and 26-0 at Mather-lane. Against these is to be put the defeat by 13-11 which Warrington sus- tained at Leigh in the second round for the Lancashire Cup. Warrington ought to win again, in fact they should secure the maximum points from all four September engagements if form is at all maintained. The prospects of the Club for the ensuing season may bedescribed as fair. Several of the men appear to be in better condition than usual, notably Fish, who scales only 12 stone Sibs. instead of 13} stones, his weight last season. He, has shown fine form in practice, and the same may be said of Dickenson, Taylor, and Tilley. The back division should be right enough,but the forward resources are not at all convincing. F. G. Jenkins is still crocked at the knee and may be of little use, and Stingers, Thomas and J. Jenkins have not yet returned from Wales. G. Heath has retired. Watkins and. S. Lees are also I doubtful starters, their injuries, having left a certain lamount of weakness. Isherwood has been training, I and may play again. There are no new captures of importance, though several men of reputation are in touch with the club. A promising forward has been secured from the Whitecross works team in Chesters, and Houghton of the Loco's has done a good trial at full back. In this position young Mclntyre of Stockton Heath has also shown capital form, and it is hoped that one of the two will provide the much-needed " A " team custodian. There will be another practice match at G o'clock this evening', when it is expected that a wing-three- quarter and a halfback from Wales will both turn cut. The team for Leigh seems likely to be : Tilley; Fish, Dickenson, Taylor and Jordan; Lloyd and Brooks; A. Boardnaan, P. Boardman, Naylor, 'Belton, Harmer, and another. The treasurer wishes VI remind the members that subscriptions for the ensuing year are now due and may be paid to him in the Pavilion on the Football Field this Saturday evening during the practice match. He will also be in attendance at Bewsey Chambers on Thursday and Friday next from 7 to 0 p.m. -- A knock-out competition has been arranged by the Warrington and District Junior Rugby League, the first round of which will commence on Tuesday next. The matches will take place on the Warrington ground. Kick-off 0.30 p.m. The firet round is as follows : - Sept. 1 St. John's v. Gorsey-lane „ 2 Greenhalgh's v Fairfield „ 3 Park Juniors v St. Elphin's „ 4 Rylands' vSt Mary's ' Harriers. . The Warrington Wesleyan Harriers are preparing for the corning season and looking forword to a good time. The annual general meeting as to be held on Tuesday next, September Ist, in the Silver-street schoolroom. Business is important, and meeting will commence at 8 p.m. prompt. It is hoped that all members and intending members will be present at the meeting.
